a: Adam, Seth, Enosh,
t: A history that starts with Adam
p: Chronicles opens with bare names: the first thirteen generations of Genesis in four verses.
b: Chronicles begins its story of Israel with the first human being. Verses 1–4 boil Genesis 5 down to a list of names with no ages, no Cain and Abel, no flood. Every reader of the time knew the stories; the list only needs to show the line. Adam is also the Hebrew word for "human," so the book opens with humanity itself before it narrows to Israel. Outside Genesis, only one other genealogy of Israel's line starts from Adam: Luke's line of Jesus, which runs backward and ends "the son of Adam, the son of God" (Luke 3:38). Matthew starts with Abraham instead (Matthew 1:1–2).

a: Noah, Shem, Ham and Japheth.
t: Noah's three sons, or a fourth generation?
p: The Hebrew lists Shem, Ham and Japheth as if they continued the single line from Adam.
b: Up to Noah the list is one name per generation. Then the Hebrew simply adds three more names, so a reader who did not know Genesis 5:32 might take Shem, Ham and Japheth as Noah's son, grandson and great-grandson. Genesis makes clear they are brothers, and the next verses treat them that way. The Greek translation smooths this by adding "the sons of Noah," and many English versions do the same. The short form is typical of these chapters: the writer assumes the reader knows Genesis.
orig: נֹחַ שֵׁם חָם וָיָפֶת (Noach Shem Cham va-Yafet)

a: Japheth's sons were Gomer, Magog, Madai, Javan, Tubal, Meshech and Tiras.
t: The nations of the world in a few lines
p: Verses 5–23 copy the Table of Nations in Genesis 10, keeping the names and dropping the comments.
b: This is Genesis 10 almost word for word, but without its notes on lands, languages and cities. The order is the same: Japheth, the far peoples of the north and the islands; Ham, the peoples of Africa and Canaan; and Shem, last, because Israel's line runs through him. Japheth's sons are the peoples later known as Cimmerians (Gomer), Medes (Madai), Ionian Greeks (Javan), and peoples of Asia Minor (Tubal, Meshech). Ezekiel 38:2 makes Magog, Meshech and Tubal the homeland of Gog. By opening with every nation, Chronicles places Israel inside the whole human family God made.

a: Diphath
p: Genesis 10:3 has Riphath. The Hebrew letters d and r look almost the same. See the variant for the witnesses.
b: In Hebrew square script, dalet (ד, d) and resh (ר, r) differ only by a tiny corner. Genesis 10:3 reads Riphath, and so do other witnesses here (see the variant). The Leningrad Codex has Diphath, and this translation gives the name as it stands there. The same pair of letters causes several of the small differences in this chapter: Rodanim and Dodanim (1:7), Hamran and Hemdan (1:41), Hadad and Hadar (1:50). None of them changes who is meant.

a: the Rodanim
p: Genesis 10:4 reads Dodanim. Chronicles' Rodanim, the people of Rhodes, is probably the older reading.
b: Here the d/r confusion runs the other way. Chronicles has Rodanim, and the Greek of Genesis 10:4 also reads "Rhodians," so many scholars think Rodanim, the people of the island of Rhodes, is the original reading in both books and Genesis' Dodanim is the slip. That fits the other names in the verse: Elishah (probably Cyprus or part of it), Tarshish (a far western port) and the Kittim (Cyprus, named for its town Kition). The Hebrew here also spells Tarshish with an extra ending, Tarshishah, which the Plain does not show.

a: He was the first to become a hero on the earth.
p: Chronicles keeps the first line about Nimrod and leaves out his kingdom in Babel and Assyria.
b: Genesis 10:8–12 says more: Nimrod was a famous hunter, his kingdom began in Babel in the land of Shinar, and he built Nineveh. Chronicles copies only the first sentence, the one that fits a list of names. Its cuts are usually of this kind: the writer keeps the line of descent and lets the reader find the stories in Genesis. The word gibbor, "hero, warrior," is the same word used later of David's mighty men (11:10).

a: Mizraim fathered the Ludim
p: Codex Vaticanus, the oldest full Greek Bible, leaves out 1:11–16 and 1:17b–23.
b: The Old Greek of Chronicles, called Paraleipomena, "things left out," survives best in Codex Vaticanus (300s AD). Vaticanus skips the descendants of Mizraim and Canaan (1:11–16) and the second half of 1:17 through 1:23, the sons of Aram and Joktan. Codex Alexandrinus has them, in a form close to the Greek of Genesis. Scholars debate whether the Greek translator's Hebrew lacked these lines, or the translator skipped what the reader could find in Genesis 10. The Hebrew of Chronicles has them, and the Plain follows the Hebrew. In these verses Chronicles' Hebrew is the same as Genesis, so the Plain uses the same wording as Genesis 10:13–14.

a: from whom the Philistines came
t: Where did the Philistines come from?
p: Here and in Genesis the Philistines come from the Casluhim, but Amos and Jeremiah say they came from Caphtor.
b: Amos 9:7 says God brought the Philistines "from Caphtor," and Jeremiah 47:4 calls them "the remnant of the coastland of Caphtor." Caphtor is usually identified with Crete or the Aegean world, which fits the archaeology: the Philistines settled the coast of Canaan in the 1100s BC with pottery and customs from the Aegean. Many scholars think the phrase "from whom the Philistines came" once followed "the Caphtorim" and slipped one name earlier, in Genesis and in Chronicles alike. Others think the Casluhim were simply one stop on the Philistines' way.

a: Meshech
p: Genesis 10:23 names Mash. Chronicles writes Meshech, the name of Japheth's son in 1:5.
b: Genesis gives Aram's fourth son as Mash. Chronicles has Meshech, a name already used for a son of Japheth (1:5). Most scholars think a scribe wrote the more familiar name, a common kind of slip; the Greek of Genesis and the Samaritan Pentateuch have a form like Mosoch (Meshech) in Genesis 10:23 too, so the two forms were mixed early. See the variant on this verse for whether Uz, Hul, Gether and Meshech are Shem's sons or Aram's.

a: the earth was split up
t: Peleg and the dividing of the earth
p: Peleg's name sounds like the Hebrew verb "divide." Readers have linked it to Babel, to canals, or to land.
b: The name Peleg and the verb niflegah, "was split," come from the same root. Chronicles repeats Genesis 10:25 word for word, so the riddle is the same. Jewish tradition links it to the scattering of the nations at Babel (Genesis 11:8–9), since Peleg's generation is about when that story falls. Some scholars point out that peleg also means "canal" in Hebrew and Akkadian and think of the irrigation channels of Mesopotamia. A modern idea that it refers to the splitting of the continents has no support in the text or in geology's timescale.

a: Ebal
p: Genesis 10:28 reads Obal. The Hebrew letters for o and e (vav and yod) are another common pair of slips.
b: Joktan's son is Obal in Genesis 10:28 and Ebal here. In the Hebrew script of the Second Temple period, vav (ו) and yod (י) were written almost alike, and scribes often confused them. Several Hebrew manuscripts of Chronicles read Obal, and the Samaritan Pentateuch has Ebal in Genesis. The same pair explains Alian for Alvan and Shephi for Shepho in 1:40. The name may be a South Arabian tribe, like most of Joktan's sons (Sheba, Ophir, Havilah, Hazarmaveth, which is the Hadramaut).

a: Shem, Arpachshad, Shelah,
t: Ten generations from Shem to Abram
p: Verses 24–27 repeat Genesis 11:10–26 as bare names. Luke 3:36 adds one more, Cainan.
b: As verses 1–4 gave ten generations from Adam to Noah, verses 24–27 give ten from Shem to Abram, the same pattern as Genesis 5 and 11. The Hebrew of Chronicles, like the Hebrew of Genesis 11:12, goes straight from Arpachshad to Shelah. The Greek of Genesis 11:12–13 inserts a Cainan between them, and Luke follows that Greek (Luke 3:36). Ancient lists were often shaped into round numbers of generations, and a name could drop out or be added in different copies.

a: Abram, who is Abraham.
p: The list stops on Abraham. From here on the chosen line narrows: Abraham, Isaac, Israel.
b: Abram's name was changed to Abraham, "father of many nations," in Genesis 17:5. Chronicles records the change in three words and then turns from all humanity to Abraham's family. Matthew begins Jesus' genealogy at this point, "son of David, son of Abraham" (Matthew 1:1), while Luke goes back past Abraham to Adam (Luke 3:34, 38). The structure of 1 Chronicles 1 is a funnel: the whole world (1:1–23), then Abraham's family (1:28–54), then Israel (2:1 onward).

a: Abraham's sons were Isaac and Ishmael.
t: Side lines first, then the main line
p: Isaac is named first, yet Ishmael's line is listed first. Chronicles clears the side branches before the chosen one.
b: Ishmael was the older son (Genesis 16:16; 21:5), but Isaac is named first because the promise ran through him (Genesis 21:12). Then the writer lists Ishmael's sons (1:29–31), Keturah's sons (1:32–33), and Esau's family and Edom (1:35–54) before coming to Israel's sons in chapter 2. Genesis does the same, giving Ishmael's family history (Genesis 25:12–18) before Isaac's (Genesis 25:19), and Esau's (Genesis 36) before Jacob's (Genesis 37:2). Sara Japhet calls this the pattern of the whole genealogy: secondary lines are told and closed, so the story can follow the main line.

a: This is their family history.
p: "Family history" translates toledot, the heading that organizes Genesis. Only here is it a heading in Chronicles.
b: Genesis is built around ten headings, "This is the family history (toledot) of..." (Genesis 2:4; 5:1; 6:9; 10:1; 11:10, 27; 25:12, 19; 36:1; 37:2). Only here does Chronicles use the word as a Genesis-style heading, for the sons of Ishmael, borrowing it from Genesis 25:12–13: a small sign that the writer has Genesis open and follows its order. Elsewhere it uses le-toledotam, "by their family lines," in its muster lists (5:7; 7:2, 4, 9; 8:28; 9:9, 34). Its own word for genealogy is hityachesh, "be enrolled" (see 4:33).

a: Jetur, Naphish and Kedemah.
p: Several of these names are known from Assyrian records as tribes of the Arabian desert.
b: Genesis 25:16 calls Ishmael's twelve sons "twelve chieftains by their clans," tribes rather than single men. Kedar and Nebaioth are named together in Isaiah 60:7, and Assyrian kings of the 700s and 600s BC fought the Qedarites and the Nabayati. Dumah and Tema are oases in northern Arabia (Isaiah 21:11–14). Jetur became the Itureans of New Testament times (Luke 3:1). Jetur and Naphish reappear in 5:19 as enemies of the tribes east of the Jordan, and Mibsam and Mishma show up as clans of Simeon (4:25).

a: Keturah, Abraham's concubine,
p: Genesis 25:1 calls Keturah a "wife"; Chronicles calls her a concubine, as Genesis 25:6 implies.
b: Genesis 25:1 says Abraham "took another wife (ishah), and her name was Keturah," but a few verses later it speaks of "the sons of his concubines" who were sent away from Isaac (Genesis 25:6). Chronicles uses the plainer label, pilegesh, a secondary wife without full rank. It is a real difference in wording, though not a contradiction, since ishah can cover both. Chronicles also drops the sons of Dedan from Genesis 25:3. Keturah's sons are desert peoples too: Midian is the best known (Exodus 2:15; Judges 6).

a: Isaac's sons were Esau and Israel.
p: Chronicles calls the patriarch Israel, not Jacob, except in one quoted psalm.
b: Genesis uses both names after God renames Jacob (Genesis 32:28; 35:10). Chronicles almost always says Israel: "These are the sons of Israel" (2:1), "Reuben, Israel's firstborn" (5:1), "Joseph son of Israel" (7:29). The only uses of "Jacob" are in the psalm David's singers sing in 16:13 and 16:17, quoted from Psalm 105. The choice suits the book's subject: the man and the people share one name, and the genealogy of the man is the roll of the nation.

a: Zephi, Gatam, Kenaz, Timna and Amalek
p: Genesis 36:12 says Timna was Eliphaz's concubine and Amalek's mother. Chronicles lists her among the sons.
b: Genesis gives Eliphaz five sons, Teman, Omar, Zepho, Gatam and Kenaz, and then explains that Timna, his concubine, bore him Amalek. Chronicles squeezes the two sentences into one list, so Timna reads like a son. Some translations repair this by reading "and of Timna, Amalek." Most commentators think the writer simply shortened Genesis, trusting the reader to know the story; others think a short phrase has fallen out. Timna is also the name of Lotan's sister (1:39) and of an Edomite chief (1:51). Zephi for Zepho is the same vav/yod slip noted at 1:22.

a: Seir's sons were Lotan, Shobal, Zibeon, Anah, Dishon, Ezer and Dishan.
p: Seir's sons were the Horites, the people of the land before Esau's family took it.
b: Genesis 36:20 calls Seir "the Horite, the people who lived in the land." Deuteronomy 2:12, 22 says Esau's descendants dispossessed the Horites, as Israel later did the Canaanites. Chronicles leaves out the word "Horite" but keeps the list, so the land of Edom has its own earlier history, as Canaan does in 1:13–16. Some scholars link the Horites with the Hurrians known from Mesopotamian and Egyptian texts; others think the name means "cave dwellers" (from chor, "hole") or is simply a local tribe.

a: Alian
p: Alian, Shephi, Homam and Hamran differ from Genesis 36 by one letter each.
b: Compare Genesis 36:22–26: Hemam (here Homam, 1:39), Alvan (here Alian), Shepho (here Shephi), Hemdan (here Hamran, 1:41), Akan (here Jaakan, 1:42). All are one-letter differences of the kinds that scribes made most often: vav and yod, dalet and resh. Most are spelling variants or copying slips, not different people. This translation keeps the spelling of the Hebrew of Chronicles, so readers can see the differences instead of having them smoothed away.

a: Dishon's sons were Uz and Aran.
p: Genesis 36:28 gives Uz and Aran to Dishan. Chronicles writes Dishon, probably a slip, since 1:38 has both names.
b: Seir had a son Dishon and a son Dishan (1:38; Genesis 36:21). Chronicles has already given Dishon's sons in 1:41. Here, where Genesis 36:28 has "the sons of Dishan," the Hebrew of Chronicles repeats Dishon. Most commentators read it as a copying slip of one vowel letter. Uz is also the name of Job's homeland (Job 1:1), which Lamentations 4:21 places in Edom.

a: before any king reigned over the people of Israel
p: Edom had a line of kings before Israel did. None of them was the son of the one before.
b: The list comes from Genesis 36:31–39. None of the eight kings succeeds his father, and each has his own city, so the list may describe chosen or elected leaders rather than a dynasty. The phrase "before any king reigned" implies that the writer knew of Israel's kings. Ibn Ezra noticed this in Genesis, and it is one of the classic clues in the debate over when Genesis took its final form. In Chronicles it also prepares the book's main subject: kings, and above all the king God chose, David. Saul's father is Kish, but a "Shaul" appears here too (1:48), an Edomite king with the same name.

a: Avith
p: The Hebrew consonants here spell Ayoth, but the Masoretes' reading note says Avith, as in Genesis 36:35.
b: The Masoretes, the Jewish scribes who fixed the vowels and reading of the Hebrew Bible (about AD 600–1000), did not change the written letters even when they thought them wrong. Instead they noted in the margin how a word should be read. The written form is the Ketiv, "what is written"; the reading is the Qere, "what is read." Here the Ketiv is Ayoth and the Qere Avith. This translation follows the Qere, the traditional reading, and notes the Ketiv where it matters (1:51; 3:24; 4:7; 6:26; 6:35; 7:1; 7:31; 7:34; 9:4; 9:35). The KJV usually follows the Qere too, but not always.

a: Hadad reigned in his place. The name of his city was Pai
t: Hadad or Hadar, Pai or Pau?
p: Genesis 36:39 has Hadar and Pau. Chronicles has Hadad and Pai, again small letter differences.
b: The last king is Hadar in the Hebrew of Genesis 36:39, though many Hebrew manuscripts and the Samaritan Pentateuch of Genesis read Hadad, the name of a storm god and of several Edomite and Aramean kings (1 Kings 11:14). Chronicles' Hadad is likely right. His city is Pau in Genesis and Pai here, a vav/yod pair. Chronicles also does not repeat "son of Achbor" when Baal-hanan dies. These are spelling variants and copying slips, not new information.
orig: הֲדַד ... פָּעִי (Hadad ... Pa'i); Genesis 36:39 הֲדַר ... פָּעוּ (Hadar ... Pa'u)

a: Then Hadad died.
p: Only Chronicles reports the last king's death. That makes the chiefs look like what followed the kings.
b: Genesis 36 does not say that Hadar died, which may mean he was still alive when the list was made. Chronicles adds "Then Hadad died" and joins the next list with "and," so the chiefs of Edom seem to come after the kings, as rulers who replaced them. In Genesis 36:40 the chiefs are a separate list, arranged "by their clans and their places." This is a real difference of presentation, perhaps reflecting the Chronicler's knowledge that Edom's kingdom had ended: after Babylon's conquests, Edomites (later called Idumeans) moved into southern Judah, around Hebron, and they were the returned exiles' neighbors.

a: These are the sons of Israel
t: Twelve sons, and Chronicles' own order
p: The list matches no other order exactly. Dan comes before Joseph, and the tribes that follow are arranged around Judah, Levi and Benjamin.
b: The twelve names follow Leah's sons (Genesis 35:23) but then put Dan, a son of Bilhah, ahead of Rachel's sons, Joseph and Benjamin. No other list does this; it may follow the birth stories of Genesis 30. The chapters that follow do not keep this order. They start with Judah (2:3–4:23), then Simeon, the tribes east of the Jordan, Levi at the center (chapter 6), the northern tribes, and Benjamin last (chapters 7–8). Zebulun gets no list at all, and Dan gets at most a line (7:12). Judah, Levi and Benjamin, the tribes of the returned community, fill most of the space.

a: Shua's daughter, the Canaanite woman
p: The Hebrew bat-shua, "Shua's daughter," can also be read as a name, Bath-shua: the same as Bathsheba's name in 3:5.
b: Genesis 38:2 says Judah married "the daughter of a Canaanite man whose name was Shua." Chronicles writes bat-Shua, which can mean "Shua's daughter" or be read as her own name, Bath-shua. In 3:5 the Hebrew calls Solomon's mother by exactly the same Hebrew, bat-shua, which the Plain there gives as the name Bath-shua, where Samuel says Bathsheba. So the first mother of Judah's tribe and the mother of Judah's greatest kings bear one name. Commentators debate whether the writer meant the echo. Either way, Judah's line begins with a Canaanite woman, and Chronicles says so openly.

a: Er, Judah's firstborn, was evil in the LORD's eyes, and the LORD put him to death.
t: The first comment: sin and death
p: The first sentence in Chronicles that is more than a name is about sin bringing death.
b: This line, copied from Genesis 38:7, is the first time Chronicles stops a list to make a point. It does not mention Onan's sin (Genesis 38:9–10), only Er's. Many scholars see here an early sign of one of the book's main ideas: God repays faithfulness and unfaithfulness within a life or a generation. The next such comment, on Achar (2:7), names the key word, ma'al, "unfaithfulness," and the same word will explain Saul's death (10:13) and the exile (9:1). Others warn against making too much of a quotation, since the writer keeps what Genesis says.

a: Tamar, his daughter-in-law, bore him Perez and Zerah.
t: Tamar in the line of David
p: Chronicles names Tamar and her relationship to Judah without comment. Matthew names her too.
b: Genesis 38 tells how Tamar, twice widowed and denied Judah's third son, disguised herself and had twins by Judah, who then said, "She is more in the right than I am" (Genesis 38:26). Chronicles sums the story up in one plain sentence. Perez is the ancestor of David (2:5, 9–15; Ruth 4:18–22). Matthew's genealogy names four women before Mary: Tamar, Rahab, Ruth and "the wife of Uriah" (Matthew 1:3–6). Chronicles names Tamar and, for Bathsheba, her own name (3:5), but not Rahab or Ruth.

a: Zimri, Ethan, Heman, Calcol and Dara
t: Famous wise men in Judah's line
p: Ethan, Heman, Calcol and Darda were the wise men Solomon outshone (1 Kings 4:31). Chronicles makes them Judahites.
b: 1 Kings 4:31 says Solomon was wiser "than Ethan the Ezrahite, than Heman and Calcol and Darda, the sons of Mahol." Chronicles lists the same names, with Dara for Darda (see the variant), as sons of Zerah. "Ezrahite" may mean "of Zerah," which would explain the link. Psalms 88 and 89 are titled for Heman and Ethan the Ezrahites. But Chronicles also has a Levite singer Heman (6:33) and a Levite Ethan (6:44), and readers have long asked whether these are the same men. Zimri is Zabdi in Joshua 7:1, likely a copying difference (see 2:7).

a: Achar, Israel's troubler
p: Joshua calls him Achan. Chronicles spells him Achar, which matches the verb "trouble" and the Valley of Achor.
b: In Joshua 7 the man who stole from Jericho's banned goods is Achan son of Carmi, son of Zabdi. Joshua says to him, "Why have you brought trouble on us? The LORD will bring trouble on you" (Joshua 7:25), and the place is named the Valley of Achor, "trouble." Chronicles writes the name as Achar, so the man's name and his deed match: Akhar okher Yisra'el, "Achar, Israel's troubler." The Greek of Joshua and Josephus also call him Achar. It may be the older form, or a deliberate play on words.

a: acted unfaithfully
t: Ma'al: the word that explains the exile
p: Ma'al, "unfaithfulness," is Chronicles' word for breaking faith with God. It explains Saul's fall and the exile.
b: Ma'al is a priestly word for taking what belongs to God or breaking trust with him (Leviticus 5:15; 6:2; Joshua 7:1). Chronicles uses it far more than any other book. Achar's theft is the first case. The tribes east of the Jordan "acted unfaithfully" and were exiled (5:25–26); Judah was exiled "because of their unfaithfulness" (9:1); Saul died "for his unfaithfulness" (10:13); Uzziah, Ahaz and Manasseh act unfaithfully (2 Chronicles 26:16; 28:19; 33:19); and the last generation of Judah "multiplied unfaithfulness" (2 Chronicles 36:14). Achar's story stands at the head of Judah's line as a warning.

a: Chelubai
p: Hezron's son Chelubai is the Caleb of 2:18. Chronicles makes Caleb's clan part of Judah through Hezron.
b: The Hebrew spells the name Kelubai here, Kalev (Caleb) in 2:18 and 2:42, and Kelub in 4:11. Elsewhere the famous spy Caleb is "son of Jephunneh the Kenizzite" (Numbers 32:12; Joshua 14:6), and Kenaz was an Edomite clan name (1:36, 53). Chronicles has both: Caleb son of Hezron here, and Caleb son of Jephunneh in 4:15. Many scholars think a clan that came from outside Israel, the Kenizzites, was adopted into Judah, and Chronicles records the adoption by giving Caleb a Judahite father. Others hold that two different Calebs are meant.

a: Ram
p: Matthew follows the Greek form Aram. Luke's best manuscripts have two names, Admin and Arni.
b: Ram stands in the line from Judah to David here and in Ruth 4:19. The Greek Old Testament writes him as Aram, and Matthew 1:3–4 follows that spelling. In Luke 3:33 the oldest manuscripts read "son of Admin, son of Arni" where later ones have "son of Aram," so Luke's line has an extra generation. Since 2:25 also names a Ram as Jerahmeel's firstborn, some scholars think Ram the brother of Jerahmeel was added to the list to link David to Hezron.

a: Nahshon, leader of the people of Judah
p: Nahshon led Judah in the wilderness, and his sister married Aaron. Judah's royal line and Levi's priestly line meet.
b: Nahshon son of Amminadab was the leader of Judah when Moses counted the tribes (Numbers 1:7; 2:3) and brought the first offering at the tabernacle's dedication (Numbers 7:12). Aaron married Elisheba, "the daughter of Amminadab and sister of Nahshon" (Exodus 6:23). So the family of David and the family of the high priests were joined from the start, a fitting detail in a book that sets king and temple side by side. Jewish legend makes Nahshon the first to step into the Sea of Reeds (Bavli Sotah 37a).

a: Salma
p: Boaz's father is Salma here, Salmah and Salmon in Ruth 4:20–21, and Salmon in Matthew and Luke.
b: The Hebrew has Salma here. Ruth spells the name two ways in two verses: Salmah (Ruth 4:20) and Salmon (Ruth 4:21); this site's Plain of Ruth uses Salmon for both. Matthew 1:4–5 has Salmon. In Luke 3:32 the critical text (NA28), following the oldest manuscripts, reads Sala; later manuscripts have Salmon. These are spelling variants of one name. Matthew alone adds that Salmon's wife was Rahab (Matthew 1:5), a detail no Old Testament text gives. Notice too that another Salma is "father of Bethlehem" in 2:51 and 2:54. Boaz lived in Bethlehem, so the two may be one clan memory.

a: Boaz fathered Obed, and Obed fathered Jesse.
p: Verses 5 and 9–15 run in the same ten generations that close the book of Ruth.
b: Ruth ends with ten names: Perez, Hezron, Ram, Amminadab, Nahshon, Salmon, Boaz, Obed, Jesse, David (Ruth 4:18–22). Chronicles has the same chain, but it names neither Ruth nor Naomi, and it gives no hint that David's great-grandmother was a Moabite. It does mention other foreign women and men in Judah's family: a Canaanite (2:3), an Ishmaelite (2:17), an Egyptian slave (2:34) and an Egyptian princess (4:18). Ten generations from Perez to David is a round number, like ten from Adam to Noah; many scholars think some names have been skipped, since the line must cover the time in Egypt.

a: Jesse fathered his firstborn
p: In this verse the Hebrew spells Jesse's name Ishai, with an extra first letter.
b: In 2:12 and elsewhere Jesse is Yishai. In this verse alone the Hebrew writes Ishai, with an alef at the start. It is only a spelling variant of the same name, so the Plain keeps the familiar form Jesse. The brothers also have variant names: Shimea here is Shammah in 1 Samuel 16:9 and 17:13, and Shimeah in 2 Samuel 13:3.

a: the seventh David
p: 1 Samuel says Jesse had eight sons. Chronicles names seven, with David the seventh.
b: In 1 Samuel 16:10–11 Jesse brings seven sons before Samuel and David is the eighth, and 1 Samuel 17:12 says Jesse "had eight sons." Chronicles names seven, with David last. Explanations: (1) one brother died young without children and was dropped from the family register (the view of several Jewish commentators); (2) the Chronicler made David the seventh, the place of honor in ancient lists, as Enoch is "seventh from Adam" (Jude 14); (3) Chronicles' own list is incomplete, since 27:18 mentions an "Elihu, one of David's brothers," whom the Syriac translation adds here. The difference is real; the text does not tell us which explanation is right.

a: Zeruiah and Abigail were their sisters.
p: Zeruiah's sons, Abishai, Joab and Asahel, were David's nephews and his toughest generals.
b: Samuel always calls them "the sons of Zeruiah," naming them by their mother, and David complains that they are "too harsh for me" (2 Samuel 3:39). Only Chronicles says outright that Zeruiah and Abigail were David's sisters. 2 Samuel 17:25 calls Abigail "Nahash's daughter," which has led some to think the sisters were half-sisters from another father, or that Nahash was another name of Jesse or of his wife. See the note on 2 Samuel 17:25.

a: Abshai
p: The Hebrew here spells Joab's brother Abshai. Samuel and most of Chronicles spell him Abishai.
b: Samuel calls him Avishai (1 Samuel 26:6; 2 Samuel 2:18). Here, and in some verses later in Chronicles, the Hebrew has the shorter form Avshai. Both mean something like "my father is Jesse" or "father of a gift." The Plain keeps each verse's spelling. It is the same man, Joab's brother and one of David's fiercest commanders.

a: Jether the Ishmaelite
p: 2 Samuel 17:25 calls Amasa's father "Ithra the Israelite." Chronicles' "Ishmaelite" is probably the original.
b: There would be no reason to say a man in Israel's army was "the Israelite," but there was good reason to note that Amasa's father was an Ishmaelite, a foreigner who married David's sister. Many scholars think Samuel's Hebrew changed one letter or that a scribe made the familiar word out of the unfamiliar one; some Greek manuscripts of Samuel also read "Ishmaelite." Jether and Ithra are two forms of one name (see the note on 1 Kings 2:5). Amasa later commanded Absalom's army and was killed by Joab (2 Samuel 20:9–10).

a: Caleb son of Hezron had children by Azubah, his wife, and by Jerioth.
p: The Hebrew literally says Caleb "fathered Azubah, a wife, and Jerioth." Something is off in the text.
b: Read literally, the Hebrew says that Caleb "fathered Azubah, a woman, and Jerioth," which cannot be right, since Azubah is his wife in 2:19. Most translations read it as "had children by Azubah his wife." Some think Jerioth was a second wife; others, following the Latin Vulgate, take Jerioth as Azubah's other name or as her daughter. "Her sons" in the next sentence fits Azubah best. The Plain gives the most likely sense and marks the uncertainty here.
orig: הוֹלִיד אֶת־עֲזוּבָה אִשָּׁה וְאֶת־יְרִיעוֹת (holid et-Azuvah ishah ve-et-Yeri'ot)

a: Uri fathered Bezalel.
p: Bezalel built the tabernacle and its furnishings. Chronicles puts him in Caleb's family.
b: God called "Bezalel son of Uri, son of Hur, of the tribe of Judah" and filled him with skill to make the tabernacle, the ark and the altars (Exodus 31:2–5; 35:30–35). Chronicles says his grandfather Hur was the son of Caleb and Ephrath, so the craftsman of Israel's first sanctuary came from Judah's leading family. Later, Solomon goes to worship at the bronze altar "that Bezalel son of Uri, son of Hur, had made" (2 Chronicles 1:5). The Chronicler likes these links between Judah and worship: the king's tribe also built the sanctuary.

a: the daughter of Machir, Gilead's father
p: Hezron's late marriage ties Judah to the clans of Gilead east of the Jordan.
b: Machir was Manasseh's son and the founder of Gilead's clans (Numbers 26:29; 32:39–40). By having Hezron marry Machir's daughter, the genealogy explains why some families of Gilead counted themselves kin to Judah. Their son Segub fathered Jair, whom Numbers 32:41 calls "Jair son of Manasseh." Both can be true in ancient terms: a man could be listed by his father's tribe or his mother's, and "son of" often means "descendant of." Genealogies like this often record alliances and settlements between clans, written as marriages and births.

a: Then Geshur and Aram seized Havvoth-jair from them
p: Havvoth-jair means "the tent villages of Jair." The Arameans later took them.
b: Numbers 32:41 and Deuteronomy 3:14 tell how Jair captured villages in Bashan and named them after himself. Judges 10:3–4 has a judge Jair with thirty towns in Gilead. Geshur was a small Aramean kingdom east of the Sea of Galilee (David married a Geshurite princess, 3:2), and Aram is Damascus. The loss probably happened during the long wars between Israel and Damascus in the 800s BC (2 Kings 10:32–33). The Chronicler keeps the note though it records a defeat: the genealogies were built from old records with their own history in them.

a: The sons of Jerahmeel
p: In David's day the Jerahmeelites were a separate clan of the Negev. Chronicles counts them as Judah.
b: When David raided from Ziklag he told Achish he had attacked "the Negev of the Jerahmeelites" (1 Samuel 27:10), and later he sent gifts to the people "in the towns of the Jerahmeelites" (1 Samuel 30:29). So the Jerahmeelites, like the Kenizzites and Kenites, were neighbors who became part of Judah. Chronicles' long Jerahmeel list (2:25–33, 42) gives them a place in the family through Hezron's firstborn. Many names here are found nowhere else.

a: Sheshan's son was Ahlai.
t: A son for a man with no sons?
p: 2:34 says Sheshan had no sons. Ahlai may be his daughter, or a descendant through his daughter.
b: This verse gives Sheshan a son, Ahlai, while 2:34 says he had only daughters. Some think Ahlai was the daughter he gave to Jarha (the name could be a woman's). Others think Ahlai was a grandson through her, counted as Sheshan's son, as Jair is counted to Hezron (2:21–22). Interestingly, one of David's warriors is "Zabad son of Ahlai" (11:41), and a Zabad appears in Sheshan's line in 2:36. Whatever the details, the point of 2:34–41 is that Sheshan's line survived through a daughter and a foreign slave.

a: He did have a slave
p: The Hebrew eved covers a slave, a servant, a royal official, or a humble "I." Here it is a slave.
b: Eved means anyone under a master. In Chronicles it can mean a royal official ("the king's servants"), a worshiper ("your servant" David, 17:4), or, as here, a slave owned by a household. Jarha is an Egyptian slave, and Sheshan marries his daughter to him so that his line will not die out. Israel's law allowed a slave to marry into the household (Exodus 21:4), and Abraham once expected his slave Eliezer to be his heir (Genesis 15:2–3). This translation says "servant" or "slave" by context.

a: Jekamiah fathered Elishama.
t: A long line through a slave's son
p: From Jarha to Elishama runs thirteen generations, one of the longest unbroken chains in the Bible.
b: Counting from Attai, this chain (2:35–41) has thirteen generations, which would carry it from about David's time to the late 700s or 600s BC if it began then. Lists like this one, giving father and son in a straight line, usually trace one family's claim to a name or a place. This one shows that the descendants of an Egyptian slave were full members of Judah, enrolled with the rest. Some scholars wonder whether this Elishama is the grandfather of Ishmael, "of the royal family," who murdered Gedaliah (Jeremiah 41:1), but that is only a guess.

a: who was the father of Ziph
p: "Father of Ziph," "father of Hebron," "father of Bethlehem": in these lists a man can father a town.
b: In 2:42–55 and 4:1–23 many "sons" are places: Ziph, Mareshah, Hebron, Tappuah, Beth-zur, Kiriath-jearim, Bethlehem, Tekoa. "Father of" (avi) means founder, chief or leading clan of a town, as one might say "the father of a country." Genealogy was the ancient way to map who belonged where. A town listed as a son of Caleb was a town where Calebite clans lived. The second half of this verse, "the sons of Mareshah, the father of Hebron," seems damaged, since we would expect Mareshah to be Caleb's second son; translations repair it in different ways.

a: Caleb's daughter was Achsah.
p: Achsah is the bride of Othniel who asked her father for pools of water (Joshua 15:16–19).
b: In Joshua and Judges, Caleb son of Jephunneh promises his daughter Achsah to whoever captures Kiriath-sepher; Othniel wins her, and she asks her father, "Give me a blessing... give me pools of water too" (Joshua 15:19; Judges 1:15). Here Achsah is the daughter of Caleb son of Hezron. The line confirms that Chronicles is drawing on the same family memories, folded into a single family tree (see 2:9). Othniel appears in 4:13.

a: Hur was the firstborn of Ephrathah
p: Ephrath(ah) is Caleb's wife and also the old name of Bethlehem's district, the home of David.
b: Caleb's wife Ephrath (2:19) is the mother of Hur, and Hur's son Salma is "father of Bethlehem" (2:51; 4:4). Ephrathah was the name of Bethlehem's district: Rachel was buried "on the way to Ephrath, which is Bethlehem" (Genesis 35:19), Elimelech's family were "Ephrathites, from Bethlehem" (Ruth 1:2), and Micah speaks to "Bethlehem Ephrathah," from which a ruler will come (Micah 5:2). Matthew quotes Micah about Jesus' birthplace (Matthew 2:6). The Hebrew of this verse reads "son of Hur," not "sons"; the Plain takes it to name Shobal as Hur's son, with Salma and Hareph after him.

a: Haroeh, half of the Menuhoth
p: Haroeh is probably Reaiah of 4:2, and the Menuhoth are probably the Manahathites of 2:54.
b: The Hebrew haro'eh can be read as "the seer," but here it is a name, very likely the Reaiah son of Shobal in 4:2 with the letters slightly changed. "Half of the Menuhoth" pairs with "half of the Manahathites" in 2:54: one clan split between two branches of the family. Manahath may be the town near Jerusalem known today as Malha, and the Benjaminites of 8:6 were taken there.

a: the Zorathites and the Eshtaolites
p: Zorah and Eshtaol were Samson's home towns, first Dan's territory, later Judah's.
b: Samson was from Zorah, and the Spirit first stirred him "between Zorah and Eshtaol" (Judges 13:2, 25). Joshua lists both towns for Dan (Joshua 19:41), and the Danites set out from there to find a new home in the north (Judges 18:2, 11). After Dan moved, Judahite clans settled the area, and Chronicles counts its people as Calebites. This is one of several places where Dan's old land appears under other tribes, while Dan itself is almost missing from the genealogies (see 7:12).

a: They are the Kenites who come from Hammath, father of Rechab's family.
p: Judah's list ends with Kenites, the clan of Moses' father-in-law, and with the Rechabites.
b: The Kenites were a desert clan; Moses' father-in-law was one (Judges 1:16; 4:11), and they settled with Judah in the Negev (Judges 1:16; 1 Samuel 27:10). The Rechabites, descendants of Jonadab son of Rechab, refused wine and lived in tents in loyalty to their ancestor, and Jeremiah held them up as a model of faithfulness (Jeremiah 35; 2 Kings 10:15). By ending Judah's family with these "clans of scribes" of Kenite origin, Chronicles again shows outsiders joined to Judah. Who the scribes were is not known; the Targum turns the three clan names into descriptions of scholars who sang and studied.

a: The second was Daniel
p: 2 Samuel 3:3 calls Abigail's son Chileab. Chronicles calls him Daniel. He may have had two names.
b: Abigail, the widow of Nabal of Carmel (1 Samuel 25), bore David a son who is Chileab in the Hebrew of 2 Samuel 3:3 and Daniel here. The Greek of Samuel has a third form, Dalouia. The Talmud says his name was Daniel and he was called Chileab because he put Mephibosheth to shame (makhlim) in debates of law (Bavli Berakhot 4a). Rashi on 2 Samuel 3:3 gives another explanation: kol-av, "all his father," because he looked exactly like David, proof that Nabal was not the father. Many scholars think one of the names was damaged in copying. Either way, he disappears from the story; he plays no part in the struggle for the throne. He is not the prophet Daniel.

a: He reigned there seven years and six months, and in Jerusalem thirty-three years.
p: Chronicles keeps Samuel's exact count of David's years in Hebron, though later it rounds to seven (29:27).
b: 2 Samuel 5:5 gives the same figures: seven and a half years in Hebron as king of Judah, thirty-three in Jerusalem over all Israel. At the end of David's life Chronicles rounds them to "seven years in Hebron and thirty-three in Jerusalem," forty in all (29:27). Notice that Chronicles mentions the Hebron years here, in the genealogy, but its story of David begins with all Israel making him king at Hebron (11:1–3), passing over the seven years when Saul's son Esh-baal ruled the north (2 Samuel 2–4).

a: Shimea
p: 2 Samuel 5:14 and 1 Chronicles 14:4 call this son Shammua. The forms are spelling variants.
b: The first son born in Jerusalem is Shammua in 2 Samuel 5:14 and in Chronicles' own second list (14:4), and Shimea here. Both come from the verb shama', "hear." The same name is given to one of David's brothers (2:13). This is a spelling variant, not a different son.

a: Nathan and Solomon
p: Matthew traces Jesus through Solomon and the kings. Luke traces him through Nathan, Solomon's brother.
b: Matthew follows the royal line, "David fathered Solomon" (Matthew 1:6), through the kings of 3:10–16. Luke's list runs through "Nathan, son of David" (Luke 3:31) and names no kings at all between David and Shealtiel. Christian readers since Julius Africanus (about AD 220) have explained the two lines in several ways: Luke gives Mary's line and Matthew Joseph's; or one line is legal, the other natural, joined by a levirate marriage; or Matthew traces the royal right and Luke the bloodline. Many modern scholars think the two evangelists drew on different family traditions and shaped them for their own purposes.

a: These four were from Bath-shua daughter of Ammiel.
p: Chronicles names Bathsheba as the mother of four sons but never tells how David took her.
b: 2 Samuel 11–12 tells of David's adultery with Bathsheba, the death of Uriah, Nathan's rebuke and the death of the first child; Solomon was born afterward (2 Samuel 12:24). Chronicles never tells this story. Here Bathsheba is simply "Bath-shua daughter of Ammiel," a spelling of her name that matches Judah's Canaanite wife (2:3), with her father's name as Ammiel instead of Eliam (2 Samuel 11:3; the two parts of the name are reversed, "my kinsman is God"). Some read the silence as cleaning up David's image; others note that the readers knew Samuel and the Chronicler assumed it. Solomon is listed fourth, though 2 Samuel suggests he was Bathsheba's first surviving son, perhaps because the most important name comes last.

a: Elishama, Eliphalet
p: The list names Elishama and Eliphelet twice each. 2 Samuel 5 has Elishua and lacks the first Eliphelet and Nogah.
b: 2 Samuel 5:14–16 lists eleven sons born in Jerusalem. Chronicles has thirteen: it adds Eliphalet and Nogah, and it has Elishama where Samuel has Elishua. Chronicles' second list (14:4–7) has Elishua and also includes Elpelet and Nogah, so the extra names were probably in the Chronicler's source. The Greek here reads Elisa (Elishua), and the first Elishama is very likely a copying slip, the scribe's eye running ahead to the Elishama of 3:8. The Hebrew also spells the first Eliphelet with a different vowel, Eliphalet. A son who died young might explain the repeated names.

a: Tamar was their sister.
p: Of all David's daughters, only Tamar is named, the sister Amnon raped (2 Samuel 13).
b: David surely had other daughters (2 Samuel 5:13), but the genealogy names only Tamar, Absalom's full sister. Her story in 2 Samuel 13 is one of the darkest in the Bible: raped by her half-brother Amnon, avenged by Absalom, and left "desolate" in her brother's house (2 Samuel 13:20). Chronicles tells none of it. Including her name may be a quiet sign that the writer knew. The phrase "apart from the concubines' sons" recalls 2 Samuel 5:13 and the ten concubines of 2 Samuel 15:16.

a: Abijah his son
p: Kings calls Rehoboam's son Abijam. Chronicles always says Abijah, "the LORD is my father."
b: 1 Kings 15:1–8 names him Abijam; Chronicles always uses Abijah, a name with the divine name in it, and tells a much kinder story about him (2 Chronicles 13). Some think Abijam is a scribal form, others that Kings avoids honoring a bad king with a pious name. See the note on 1 Kings 14:31. Matthew 1:7 has Abijah (Greek Abia).

a: Joram his son, Ahaziah his son, Joash his son,
p: Matthew 1:8 jumps from Joram to Uzziah, leaving out Ahaziah, Joash and Amaziah. Chronicles has them all.
b: The list in 3:10–14 gives every king of Judah from Solomon to Josiah except Athaliah, the queen who seized the throne (2 Kings 11), since she was not a son. Matthew's genealogy says "Joram fathered Uzziah" (Matthew 1:8), skipping three kings, so that the period from David to the exile has fourteen generations (Matthew 1:17). Early readers noticed: Jerome suggested the three were removed because they descended from wicked Jezebel through Athaliah. Most scholars think Matthew shaped the list into three sets of fourteen on purpose; fourteen is the number value of David's name in Hebrew (D+W+D = 4+6+4).

a: Azariah his son
p: This king has two names: Azariah in most of Kings, Uzziah in Chronicles' story, Isaiah and Matthew.
b: Kings mostly calls him Azariah (2 Kings 14:21; 15:1–7), but sometimes Uzziah (2 Kings 15:13, 30). The story in Chronicles calls him Uzziah (2 Chronicles 26), as do Isaiah 6:1, Amos 1:1 and Matthew 1:8–9. The two names are related: azar and oz both have to do with help and strength. Here, in the list, Chronicles uses the form from Kings.

a: the firstborn, Johanan; the second, Jehoiakim; the third, Zedekiah; the fourth, Shallum.
p: Johanan is otherwise unknown, and Shallum is King Jehoahaz. The order is not their order of birth.
b: Three of Josiah's sons became kings: Shallum, who took the throne name Jehoahaz (2 Kings 23:30–31; Jeremiah 22:11); Jehoiakim, first named Eliakim (2 Kings 23:34); and Zedekiah, first named Mattaniah (2 Kings 24:17). Johanan, called the firstborn, is mentioned nowhere else and probably died young. The ages in Kings make Jehoiakim the oldest of the three kings and Zedekiah the youngest, so listing Shallum last, after Zedekiah, does not follow birth order. Perhaps the list ranks Zedekiah, the last king, with his full brother Shallum (both sons of Hamutal, 2 Kings 23:31; 24:18) in an order the writer had his reasons for.

a: Jeconiah his son, Zedekiah his son.
p: This Zedekiah is called Jehoiakim's son. He may be a son of Jehoiakim, or King Zedekiah counted as Jeconiah's successor.
b: King Zedekiah was Josiah's son and Jeconiah's uncle (2 Kings 24:17; 3:15). 2 Chronicles 36:10 calls him Jeconiah's "brother," which may mean "relative." So who is this Zedekiah? (1) A different man, a son of Jehoiakim and brother of Jeconiah, otherwise unknown. (2) King Zedekiah, listed after Jeconiah because he followed him on the throne, "his son" meaning "his successor." Jeconiah is the same king as Jehoiachin (2 Kings 24:6) and Coniah (Jeremiah 22:24); the names mean "the LORD establishes."

a: The sons of Jeconiah, who was taken captive
p: Babylonian ration tablets name Jehoiachin, "king of Judah," and five of his sons in Babylon.
b: Jeconiah (Jehoiachin) surrendered to Nebuchadnezzar in 597 BC and was taken to Babylon (2 Kings 24:12–15). Clay tablets found in the ruins of Babylon's palace, published by Ernst Weidner in 1939, record oil rations for "Ya'u-kinu, king of the land of Yahudu" and for five sons of the king of Judah, about 592 BC. Some read the Hebrew assir as a name, "Assir" (KJV), making him another son; most take it as "captive." Jeremiah had said of Coniah, "none of his offspring will succeed" on David's throne (Jeremiah 22:30), yet the line continued here, and his grandson Zerubbabel led the return (see 3:19).

a: Shealtiel his son
t: After the exile, Matthew and Luke part ways
p: Both Gospels name Shealtiel and Zerubbabel, but neither gives Zerubbabel a son listed here.
b: Matthew 1:12 says "Jeconiah fathered Shealtiel, and Shealtiel fathered Zerubbabel"; Luke 3:27 calls Shealtiel the son of Neri, not Jeconiah. After Zerubbabel the two Gospels name Abiud (Matthew 1:13) and Rhesa (Luke 3:27), neither of whom is among Zerubbabel's children in 3:19–20. Chronicles is the only Old Testament source for David's line after Zerubbabel, and the Gospels follow other family records for the centuries between.

a: Shenazzar
p: Some identify Shenazzar with Sheshbazzar, "the leader of Judah" who brought the temple vessels back (Ezra 1:8).
b: Ezra 1:8–11 says Cyrus had the temple vessels counted out to "Sheshbazzar, the leader of Judah," and Ezra 5:14–16 says he laid the temple's foundations. Since the two names are both Babylonian and look alike, many have thought Shenazzar, Jeconiah's son, is the same man; that would make the first leader of the return Zerubbabel's uncle. Others reject the link because the names are spelled differently in a way that is hard to explain. Babylonian names such as Shenazzar (Sin-usur, "Sin, protect") show the family had lived in Babylon long enough to use them.

a: with Shelomith their sister
p: A seal from the Persian period names "Shelomith, maidservant of Elnathan the governor." She may be this woman.
b: Zerubbabel's daughter is named, which is rare in these lists. In 1976 Nahman Avigad published a hoard of seals and seal impressions from Persian-period Judah, among them a seal of "Shelomith, amah of Elnathan the governor." Eric Meyers and others suggested that this Shelomith was Zerubbabel's daughter, married to or serving a later governor, which would explain why her name was worth recording. The link is possible but not proven, and the seal's origin and date are debated.

a: Jushab-hesed
p: Zerubbabel's children carry names of hope after the exile: "Loyal love returns," "the LORD blesses."
b: Yushav-chesed means "loyal love will be returned" or "loyal love returns." His brothers' names are also prayers and confessions: Berechiah, "the LORD blesses"; Hasadiah, "the LORD is loyal"; Hashubah, "considered"; Hananiah, "the LORD is gracious"; and Meshullam, "repaid" or "made whole." Hesed is the covenant word this translation renders "loyal love." A family that had lost its throne named its children after God's faithfulness.

a: six
p: The verse names five sons of Shemaiah but counts six. A name may have dropped out, or Shemaiah himself is counted.
b: The total "six" does not match the five names. Some count Shemaiah with his five sons; others think one name has fallen out in copying. Hattush may be the Hattush "of the sons of David" who came back with Ezra (Ezra 8:2–3), which would help date this list, but the identification is uncertain.

a: The sons of Elioenai
t: How far does David's line go?
p: Counting the generations after Jeconiah dates this list, and so Chronicles, to about 400 BC or later.
b: The Hebrew gives about six generations after Zerubbabel, who was active about 520 BC: Hananiah, Shecaniah, Shemaiah, Neariah, Elioenai and his seven sons. At roughly twenty to twenty-five years a generation, that reaches about 400 BC or a little later. The Greek reading of 3:21, which makes more generations (see the variant there), would push it later still. This is one of the main clues for dating Chronicles to the late Persian or early Greek period. Some scholars think the list was extended by later scribes after the book was written.

a: Anani
p: The Targum of Chronicles says the last name in David's line, Anani, is "the King Messiah who is to be revealed."
b: Anani sounds like anan, "cloud." The Targum, the Aramaic paraphrase of Chronicles, says of him, "he is the King Messiah who is to be revealed," linking him to Daniel's vision of "one like a son of man" coming "with the clouds of heaven" (Daniel 7:13). A midrash on Genesis gives the same reading (Tanchuma, Toledot 14). It is a beautiful example of the rabbinic habit of finding hope in a list of names: the last descendant of David in Scripture points to the king still to come. In the plain sense, Anani is simply a son of Elioenai.

a: Perez, Hezron, Carmi, Hur and Shobal
p: These five are not all Judah's sons. They are a chain of descent: son, grandson, and on down.
b: "Sons" here means descendants. Perez was Judah's son (2:4), Hezron Perez's (2:5), Hur Caleb's (2:19), Shobal Hur's (2:50). Carmi is a puzzle: elsewhere he is Achar's father (2:7) or a son of Reuben (5:3). Many commentators think Carmi stands for Chelubai, that is, Caleb (2:9), with the letters slightly changed. So the verse traces Judah to Shobal, whose descendants come in 4:2.

a: Jabez had more honor than his brothers.
t: A story in the middle of a list
p: Without warning, the list stops for a man with no father named and a prayer that God answered.
b: Jabez appears from nowhere: no father, no clan, no place, though a town of Jabez is mentioned in 2:55. Two verses tell what made him different. The pattern of a name explained by a birth ("his mother named him... saying") recalls the births of Israel's ancestors in Genesis (Genesis 29:32–35; 35:18). Interruptions like this are rare in the genealogies, and each one teaches something: Er's death (2:3), Achar's sin (2:7), the eastern tribes' prayer in battle (5:20). Nikhbad, "honored, respected," is from the root kaved, "heavy, weighty."

a: "I gave birth in pain,"
t: A name that sounds like pain
p: Jabez (Ya'bets) is almost the word for pain ('otsev) with two letters swapped. His name was a bad omen.
b: His mother explains the name with be-'otsev, "in pain." The name Ya'bets has the same letters, with the last two reversed. In the ancient world a name was thought to shape a life, and a name meaning "he causes pain" was a heavy thing to carry. The word for pain recalls the curse on the woman in Eden: "in pain you will give birth to children" (Genesis 3:16). Jabez's prayer in the next verse uses the same root again, asking that harm "not hurt me" (le-vilti 'otsbi). He prays against his own name.

a: "If you will truly bless me and widen my borders,"
p: The Hebrew is an unfinished vow: "If you..." with no "then I will..." Most versions turn it into a wish.
b: Jacob vowed, "If God will be with me... then the LORD will be my God" (Genesis 28:20–21). A vow normally has two halves: what the person asks and what he promises. Jabez's prayer has only the first half. The Hebrew im, "if," with no second half can also express a strong wish, "Oh, if only," and most translations take it that way. The Plain keeps the "if" and the trailing-off, since that is what the Hebrew does. Either way, Jabez promises God nothing; he simply asks. The doubled verb, barekh tevarakheni, "bless, you will bless me," means "truly bless me."

a: widen my borders
p: In context Jabez asks for more land. The modern "Prayer of Jabez" reads it as asking for wider influence.
b: Gevul means a border or the territory inside it, and in these chapters land is the constant concern: Simeon looks for pasture (4:39–41), the eastern tribes spread to the Euphrates (5:9–10). In Bruce Wilkinson's best seller The Prayer of Jabez (2000), "enlarge my territory" became a daily prayer for greater opportunity and ministry, and millions of readers prayed it. Supporters say it encourages bold, specific prayer and trust that God answers. Critics, including many evangelical scholars, say it treats a single verse as a formula for success and reads modern hopes into an ancient request for land. Both sides agree the verse shows God answering a man who asked.

a: if your hand is with me, and if you keep harm away so that it does not hurt me
p: The Talmud identifies Jabez with the judge Othniel and reads his prayer as a request for Torah and students.
b: The rabbis, puzzled that Jabez has no father and that a town is named after him (2:55), identified him with Othniel, Caleb's nephew (4:13; Judges 3:9). The Talmud reads each phrase as a scholar's prayer: "bless me" with Torah, "widen my borders" with students, "your hand with me" so that my learning is not forgotten, "keep harm away" (read as re'im, "companions") by giving me companions like myself, and "so that it does not hurt me" so that the evil inclination does not trouble me (Bavli Temurah 16a). The Targum of Chronicles reads the prayer in a related way, asking for children and disciples. In this tradition the "clans of scribes living at Jabez" (2:55) were his disciples.

a: And God brought about what he asked.
p: The short answer is a theme of Chronicles: God hears those who cry to him (5:20; 2 Chronicles 7:14; 33:13).
b: Chronicles keeps returning to answered prayer. The eastern tribes "shouted" to God in battle and he was moved by their pleas (5:20). God promises Solomon that if his people "pray and seek my face and turn," he will hear (2 Chronicles 7:14). Asa, Jehoshaphat and Hezekiah pray and are rescued (2 Chronicles 14:11; 20:5–12; 32:20–21), and even Manasseh, the worst of kings, prays in exile and is restored (2 Chronicles 33:12–13). Jabez is the first of these, a man who called on "the God of Israel" and was heard.

a: The sons of Kenaz: Othniel
p: Othniel son of Kenaz captured Debir, married Caleb's daughter Achsah, and became Israel's first judge.
b: Othniel won Achsah by taking Kiriath-sepher (Joshua 15:16–17; Judges 1:12–13), and later the LORD raised him up to rescue Israel from Cushan-rishathaim (Judges 3:9–11). He is "son of Kenaz, Caleb's younger brother," so the Kenizzite family of Caleb (see 2:9; 4:15) produced Israel's first judge. The Talmud identifies Othniel with Jabez (see 4:10).

a: The sons of Caleb son of Jephunneh
p: This is the famous Caleb, the faithful spy. His family descends from Kenaz, a name with Edomite roots.
b: Caleb son of Jephunneh was one of the two spies who trusted God (Numbers 13:30; 14:24) and received Hebron (Joshua 14:13–14). Numbers 32:12 and Joshua 14:6 call him a Kenizzite, and Kenaz is an Edomite clan (1:36; 1:53; Genesis 36:11, 42). The Hebrew at the end of this verse is odd, "the sons of Elah: and Kenaz," as if a name has dropped out before "and." Chronicles thus records two Caleb lines: the clan tradition that made Caleb a son of Hezron (2:18–24, 42–50) and the older memory of Caleb the Kenizzite. A group of outsiders became the heart of Judah.

a: She conceived Miriam, Shammai and Ishbah
p: "She" has no name in this verse. The sentence probably belongs after the end of 4:18, where Bithiah is named.
b: The Hebrew says "she conceived" without saying who. The end of 4:18, "These were sons of Bithiah... whom Mered had taken," fits best right before it: Mered married Bithiah, and she bore Miriam, Shammai and Ishbah. Several translations move the sentence. The Greek solves the problem differently, reading "and Jether fathered Miriam" (see the variant). The Plain keeps the Hebrew order, since moving text is a guess, and explains it here. On this reading Mered had two wives: Bithiah the Egyptian and an unnamed Judean (4:18).

a: These were sons of Bithiah, the daughter of Pharaoh
p: Mered of Judah married Bithiah, "daughter of Pharaoh." Her name means "daughter of the LORD."
b: Kings of Egypt rarely gave daughters to foreigners, and when Solomon married a pharaoh's daughter it was news (1 Kings 3:1). "Pharaoh's daughter" here may mean a woman of the Egyptian court rather than a princess. Her name, Bityah, means "daughter of Yah," a Hebrew name, perhaps taken when she joined Israel. Mered's other wife is called "the Judean" (ha-Yehudiyyah), to set her apart. The list shows again that Judah's family included Egyptians (see 2:34).

a: His Judean wife
t: Moses' rescuer in the family of Judah
p: The rabbis identified Bithiah with the princess who saved Moses, and read Jered, Heber and Jekuthiel as names of Moses.
b: The midrash noticed that a "daughter of Pharaoh" with a name meaning "daughter of God" married into Israel, and identified her with the princess who drew Moses out of the Nile (Exodus 2:5–10). God said to her, the rabbis taught, "Moses was not your son, yet you called him your son; you are not my daughter, yet I call you my daughter" (Leviticus Rabbah 1:3). The Talmud adds that she is called "the Judean" because she rejected idolatry, and that Jered, Heber and Jekuthiel are all names of Moses, whom she raised (Bavli Megillah 13a). Mered was taken to be Caleb. It is a homily, not history, but it shows how carefully these lists were read.

a: the clans of the linen workers' house at Beth-ashbea
p: Some clans of Judah were trades: craftsmen (4:14), linen workers (4:21), potters (4:23), scribes (2:55).
b: In the ancient Near East a craft was often a family business, and a clan could be a guild. Chronicles names a valley of craftsmen (4:14), a "house" of workers in buts, fine linen (4:21), royal potters (4:23) and clans of scribes (2:55). Buts is a late word for fine linen (Ezekiel 27:16; Esther 1:6), the cloth Chronicles says David and the Levites wore (15:27) and the temple veil was made of (2 Chronicles 3:14). Lists like these may come from records of the royal workforce. Shelah's son Er is named after his uncle, Judah's firstborn (2:3), a way of keeping a dead man's name alive.

a: who ruled in Moab, and Jashubi-lehem
t: Ruled in Moab, or married into Moab?
p: Ba'alu can mean "ruled" or "married"; Jashubi-lehem can be a name or "returned to Lehem." The rabbis heard Ruth's story here.
b: The verb ba'al means "be master of," and also "take as wife" (a husband is a ba'al). So Joash and Saraph either ruled in Moab or married Moabite women. Yashuvi Lachem is pointed by the Masoretes as a name, but the consonants can be read "and they returned to Lehem," that is, Bethlehem. The Talmud reads the whole verse as a coded story of Ruth: Joash and Saraph are Mahlon and Chilion, who "married into Moab," and "Jashubi-lehem" is Ruth, who "returned" and clung to Bethlehem (Bavli Bava Batra 91b). The plain sense is uncertain; the Plain follows the Masoretic pointing.
orig: אֲשֶׁר־בָּעֲלוּ לְמוֹאָב וְיָשֻׁבִי לָחֶם (asher-ba'alu le-Mo'av ve-Yashuvi Lachem)

a: These records are old.
p: The writer says outright that this material is ancient. Chronicles often names its sources.
b: Ha-devarim attiqim can mean "the records are ancient" or "the matters are old." It is a rare moment when the writer comments on his material, telling the reader that this part of the list comes from old documents. Chronicles often names sources: "the Book of the Kings of Israel" (9:1), the records of Samuel, Nathan and Gad (29:29), and others. The Talmud, reading for hidden meaning, took attiqim as a hint at "the Ancient of Days" (Daniel 7:9), saying these words were spoken by God himself (Bavli Bava Batra 91b).

a: They stayed there with the king, doing his work.
p: Royal potters worked for the crown. Stamped jar handles reading "belonging to the king" have been found across Judah.
b: Netaim ("plantings") and Gederah ("walled pen") were probably villages in the Shephelah, the low hills of western Judah, a region of clay and kilns. Well over a thousand jar handles stamped lmlk, "belonging to the king," with the name of one of four towns, have been found in Judah, most dating to Hezekiah's reign (late 700s BC). Some scholars have linked such royal workshops with the potters of this verse. The connection cannot be proven, but it shows that "working for the king" was a real job in Judah. The KJV, taking the place names as words, has "those that dwelt among plants and hedges."

a: The sons of Simeon: Nemuel, Jamin, Jarib, Zerah and Shaul;
p: Genesis and Exodus have Jemuel, Ohad, Jachin and Zohar. Chronicles is closest to Numbers 26.
b: Genesis 46:10 and Exodus 6:15: Jemuel, Jamin, Ohad, Jachin, Zohar, Shaul. Numbers 26:12–13: Nemuel, Jamin, Jachin, Zerah, Shaul. Chronicles: Nemuel, Jamin, Jarib, Zerah, Shaul. Chronicles follows Numbers in dropping Ohad and in Nemuel and Zerah, which are spelling variants of Jemuel and Zohar. Jarib for Jachin is a copying slip of the kind seen often in these lists (the letters for k and r look alike in some scripts). Genesis' note that Shaul was "the son of a Canaanite woman" is left out.

a: Mibsam his son, Mishma his son
p: Mibsam and Mishma are also sons of Ishmael (1:29–30). Simeon lived among the desert tribes and absorbed some of them.
b: Simeon's land was inside Judah's, in the Negev around Beersheba (Joshua 19:1–9), the border with the Arabian desert. Two of its clans have the same names as Ishmael's sons, Mibsam and Mishma (1:29–30; Genesis 25:13–14). Many scholars think Ishmaelite clans joined Simeon or intermarried with it, and the genealogy records that by placing them in Simeon's line. It is another sign that "Israel" in these chapters is a family that took in others.

a: their clan as a whole never grew to match Judah's numbers
p: Simeon was large in the wilderness but small later, absorbed into Judah. Moses' blessing leaves it out.
b: Simeon had 59,300 men at the first census (Numbers 1:23) and 22,200 at the second (Numbers 26:14), the steepest fall of any tribe, perhaps because of the plague after Baal-peor (Numbers 25:14 names a Simeonite leader). Jacob's dying words said of Simeon and Levi, "I will divide them among Jacob and spread them thin through Israel" (Genesis 49:7). Joshua gives Simeon towns inside Judah (Joshua 19:1, 9), and Moses' blessing in Deuteronomy 33 does not mention Simeon at all. Chronicles explains the small size with a family detail: Shimei had many children, his brothers few.

a: They lived in Beersheba, Moladah, Hazar-shual,
p: The towns match Joshua 19:2–8 with a few spelling changes and two different names.
b: Compare Joshua 19:2–7: Beersheba, Sheba, Moladah, Hazar-shual, Balah, Ezem, Eltolad, Bethul, Hormah, Ziklag, Beth-marcaboth, Hazar-susah, Beth-lebaoth, Sharuhen; Ain, Rimmon, Ether, Ashan. Chronicles has Bilhah for Balah, Tolad for Eltolad, Bethuel for Bethul and Hazar-susim for Hazar-susah, all spelling variants. Beth-biri and Shaaraim for Beth-lebaoth and Sharuhen may be real differences: other names for the same towns, or different towns of a later time. Chronicles adds Tochen and Etam in 4:32.

a: These were their towns up to the time David reigned.
p: Under David the Simeonite towns came under Judah. Ziklag had already been given to David (1 Samuel 27:6).
b: Achish of Gath gave David the town of Ziklag, "This is how Ziklag came to belong to the kings of Judah, as it still does today" (1 Samuel 27:6). When David became king of Judah at Hebron, the Negev towns of Simeon became part of his kingdom, and Simeon lost its separate standing. The note tells the reader that this list describes Simeon before David, the last time it was a tribe with towns of its own.

a: they had their own family register
p: Chronicles' key word for genealogy means "be enrolled." After the exile, being in the register meant belonging.
b: The verb hityachesh, "to be enrolled by family," and its noun yachas appear almost only in Chronicles, Ezra and Nehemiah, about twenty times. It is late Hebrew, the language of the Persian period. Ezra 2:62 shows why it mattered: priests who "searched for their family records" and could not find them were barred from the priesthood. In the returned community, a family register proved who belonged to Israel, who could serve at the altar and who could claim land. The genealogies of 1 Chronicles 1–9 are, in part, that kind of register for all Israel.

a: The people who had lived there before were from Ham.
t: Who were the people of Ham?
p: "From Ham" may mean Egyptians or Cushites, or Canaanites, all sons of Ham in 1:8.
b: Ham's sons are Cush, Mizraim (Egypt), Put and Canaan (1:8). Near Gerar, in the western Negev, Egyptian presence was strong in many periods, and 2 Chronicles 14:9–15 tells of a Cushite army defeated as far as Gerar in Asa's day. So the people "from Ham" may have been Egyptian or Cushite herders, or Canaanites. The Greek reading "Gerar" in 4:39 (see the variant) fits this setting. The description of the land, "wide on every side, quiet and at peace," echoes Laish before the Danites took it (Judges 18:7–10).

a: the Meunites they found there
p: The Meunites were a desert people of the south. The Greek calls them Minaeans, the South Arabian traders.
b: The Meunites appear again as enemies of Uzziah (2 Chronicles 26:7) and, in the Greek, of Jehoshaphat (2 Chronicles 20:1), and some of their descendants became temple servants (Ezra 2:50). The Greek translation calls them Minaioi, the Minaeans of South Arabia, who ran the incense trade in the Persian period; others link them with Maon near Petra. The written Hebrew here (Ketiv) spells the name Meinites. The phrase "put them under the ban" is cherem, the total destruction of holy war (Deuteronomy 7:2; Joshua 6:21), reported here as a fact without comment.

a: They struck down the survivors who had escaped from Amalek
p: This is the Bible's last report of fighting Amalek, the people God swore to blot out (Exodus 17:14–16).
b: Amalek attacked Israel in the wilderness, and God vowed war on Amalek "one generation after another" (Exodus 17:16; Deuteronomy 25:17–19). Saul spared Agag and the best of Amalek (1 Samuel 15); David fought Amalekite raiders (1 Samuel 30) and took their plunder (2 Samuel 8:12). Here, in Hezekiah's day, Simeonites finish off "the survivors" in Edom's hill country. Later Jewish tradition kept Amalek alive as a symbol through Haman "the Agagite" (Esther 3:1), but in the Old Testament's story this is Amalek's end.

a: but he made his father's bed unclean
p: Reuben slept with Bilhah, his father's concubine (Genesis 35:22), and Jacob took away his place as firstborn.
b: The story is told in one line in Genesis 35:22, and Jacob's dying words remember it: "you went up onto your father's bed. Then you defiled it" (Genesis 49:4). Chronicles uses the same verb, chillel, "make profane, defile." Sleeping with a father's wife or concubine was a claim to the father's place, as Absalom's public act showed (2 Samuel 16:21–22). The Chronicler explains why Israel's firstborn does not come first in his lists.

a: So his birthright went to the sons of Israel's son Joseph
t: Birthright to Joseph, rule to Judah
p: Chronicles splits the firstborn's rights in two: the birthright to Joseph, leadership to Judah.
b: Genesis never says in so many words that Joseph received Reuben's birthright, but it implies it: Jacob adopted Joseph's two sons as his own, "as much as Reuben and Simeon" (Genesis 48:5), so Joseph received a double share, the firstborn's portion (Deuteronomy 21:17). Chronicles spells it out and then adds: "Judah grew strong among his brothers, and a ruler came from him" (5:2). So the genealogy can put Judah first without denying Joseph's rights. Judah has the ruler, Joseph the birthright, and Reuben, the eldest, comes third in the lists.

a: a ruler came from him
p: Nagid, "ruler," is the word for David as God's chosen leader. Jacob's blessing promised Judah the scepter.
b: The word is nagid, which this translation renders "ruler" when it means a leader chosen by God. God told David he would be ruler over his people Israel (11:2; 17:7), and David later says God chose Judah as ruler (28:4). Behind it stands Jacob's blessing: "The scepter will not leave Judah" (Genesis 49:10). Jewish and Christian readers alike have read that blessing as messianic; the Targums and Matthew's "son of David" both draw on it. Chronicles here gives the reason the book is shaped around Judah and David.

a: Tilgath-pilneser
p: Chronicles spells the Assyrian king's name Tilgath-pilneser; Kings has Tiglath-pileser. Both render Tukulti-apil-Esharra.
b: The Assyrian king Tiglath-pileser III (reigned 745–727 BC) is called Tukulti-apil-Esharra in his own inscriptions. Kings writes Tiglat Pil'eser; Chronicles writes Tilgat Pilne'eser here and in 5:26 and 2 Chronicles 28:20. The swapped letters are a spelling variant that the Chronicler's tradition kept. His inscriptions record campaigns in 734–732 BC in which he took Gilead and Galilee and deported their people (2 Kings 15:29), the deportation this verse remembers.
orig: תִּלְּגַת פִּלְנְאֶסֶר (Tillegat Pilne'eser); 2 Kings 15:29 תִּגְלַת פִּלְאֶסֶר (Tiglat Pil'eser)

a: He lived in Aroer and as far as Nebo and Baal-meon.
p: The Moabite Stone, about 840 BC, names Nebo and Baal-meon and tells how Moab took them back from Israel.
b: The inscription of Mesha king of Moab (2 Kings 3:4), found at Dhiban in 1868, boasts that Mesha built Baal-meon, captured Nebo from Israel and slaughtered its people, and built Aroer and the road by the Arnon. It also says "the men of Gad had lived in the land of Ataroth from of old." It does not mention Reuben. These towns lay on the plateau east of the Dead Sea that Numbers 32:37–38 gives to Reuben, but by the 800s BC the area was disputed and often Moabite (Isaiah 15:2; Jeremiah 48:22–23). Reuben seems to have faded early as a separate tribe.

a: the Hagrites
p: The Hagrites were a desert people east of Gilead, named with Ishmaelites in Psalm 83:6. Their name recalls Hagar.
b: Psalm 83:6 lists "Edom's tents and the Ishmaelites, Moab and the Hagrites" among Israel's enemies. The name suggests descent from Hagar, Ishmael's mother, and in 5:19 they fight alongside Jetur and Naphish, two of Ishmael's sons (1:31). Tiglath-pileser III's inscriptions list a tribe called the Hagaranu among Aramean tribes along the Tigris and in Babylonia; the Hagrites may possibly be related to them. One of David's officials, in charge of his flocks, was Jaziz the Hagrite (27:31).

a: Sharon's pasturelands
t: A Sharon east of the Jordan
p: Not the coastal plain of Sharon, but a district east of the Jordan, also named on the Moabite Stone.
b: The famous Sharon is the plain along the Mediterranean coast (Isaiah 35:2; Song of Songs 2:1). This one is east of the Jordan, in Gad's territory, perhaps the open grazing land of the plateau. The Moabite Stone mentions "the men of Sharon" whom Mesha settled in a captured town, which confirms a Sharon in this region. "Pasturelands" (migreshe) are the open fields around towns used for grazing, the same word used for the Levites' lands in chapter 6.

a: when Jotham was king of Judah and Jeroboam was king of Israel
p: The Gadite list comes from a registration made when Jotham and Jeroboam II both reigned, about 750 BC.
b: This must be Jeroboam II of Israel (about 788–747 BC), whose reign overlapped with the early years of Jotham of Judah (about 750–735, at first as regent for his father Uzziah, 2 Kings 15:5). Under Jeroboam II Israel's borders reached their widest (2 Kings 14:25), and a register of Gilead's clans would fit that time. Some scholars doubt that a northern and a southern king held one census together and think two separate records are meant. Either way, the Chronicler is pointing to an official record behind his list.

a: he let himself be moved by their pleas
p: The verb na'tor means "let oneself be entreated." God allowed himself to be persuaded by prayer.
b: Na'tor is a passive form of atar, "to plead." It means God "let himself be pleaded with" and gave in. It is used when Isaac prayed for Rebekah to have a child (Genesis 25:21), when God heard the land's prayers after David's census (2 Samuel 24:25) and, most famously, when Manasseh prayed in exile and God "let himself be moved" and brought him home (2 Chronicles 33:13). The battle report turns into a lesson about faith: "since they had put their trust in him." The war was won by prayer, not by the 44,760.

a: 100,000 people
p: 50,000 camels and 100,000 captives are enormous for a tribal war. Readers explain the numbers in different ways.
b: The figures here, as in the army counts of chapter 7, are very large. Some readers take them at face value. Others note that the Hebrew elef, "thousand," also means a clan or a military unit (Judges 6:15; 1 Samuel 10:19), so the figures may once have counted units, not individuals. Others see round numbers used to show the size of a victory God gave. Large numbers are common in Chronicles, especially in battles (2 Chronicles 13:3, 17).

a: since the war came from God
p: The victory was God's battle, but the same tribes later lost their land for unfaithfulness.
b: "The war came from God" is a short form of a belief that runs through Chronicles: "The battle does not belong to you. It belongs to God" (2 Chronicles 20:15), echoing David to Goliath, "The battle belongs to the LORD" (1 Samuel 17:47). For the Chronicler, faith brings victory (5:20) and unfaithfulness brings defeat and exile (5:25–26). The two halves of this chapter illustrate both. Some readers find a hard lesson in the idea that God sends war; others note that the text describes Israel's defense of its land and pasture, not conquest for its own sake.

a: Baal-hermon, Senir and Mount Hermon
p: Senir is the Amorite name for Mount Hermon (Deuteronomy 3:9). Here the names mark Manasseh's northern edge.
b: Deuteronomy 3:9 explains, "The Sidonians call Hermon Sirion, and the Amorites call it Senir." Baal-hermon was probably a sacred site on its slopes (Judges 3:3). The half-tribe of Manasseh held the land from Bashan, the rich plateau east of the Sea of Galilee, up to the foot of Hermon, Israel's highest mountain. Song of Songs 4:8 calls it "the peak of Senir and Hermon."
r: Deuteronomy 3:8–9; Judges 3:3; Song of Songs 4:8; Psalm 133:3

a: They went after the gods of the land's peoples like a prostitute
p: Zanah, "act as a prostitute," pictures idolatry as breaking a marriage vow.
b: Zanah achare, "go like a prostitute after," is a picture the prophets and Judges use often: Israel is God's wife, and serving other gods is adultery (Judges 2:17; Hosea 1:2; Jeremiah 3:6–9; Ezekiel 16). Chronicles pairs it here with its own word ma'al, "act unfaithfully" (see 2:7). The verse turns the eastern tribes' story upside down: those who once trusted God in battle (5:20) and settled in the Hagrites' land (5:22) lost it the same way the Canaanites had.

a: the spirit of Pul king of Assyria, and the spirit of Tilgath-pilneser king of Assyria
p: Pul was Tiglath-pileser III's name as king of Babylon. Chronicles' "and" may mean "that is," or the writer took them as two.
b: Babylonian sources call Tiglath-pileser III by the throne name Pulu, which he used as king of Babylon from 729 BC. 2 Kings 15:19 and 15:29 mention "Pul" and "Tiglath-pileser" in separate stories without saying they are one man. Here the Hebrew joins them with ve-, "and," but follows with a singular verb, "he carried them into exile." The ve- can mean "that is" (as BSB takes it), or the Chronicler may have thought of two kings. The Plain keeps "and" and leaves the reader to weigh it. Notice the verb: God "roused the spirit" of a foreign king, the same words used of Cyrus in the last verses of Chronicles (2 Chronicles 36:22).
orig: אֶת־רוּחַ פּוּל ... וְאֶת־רוּחַ תִּלְּגַת פִּלְנֶסֶר (et-ruach Pul ... ve-et-ruach Tillegat Pilneser)

a: Halah, Habor, Hara and the river of Gozan
p: Kings places Israel's exiles in Halah, by the Habor River of Gozan, and the towns of Media. Chronicles adds Hara.
b: 2 Kings 17:6 and 18:11 say the king of Assyria settled the people of Samaria "in Halah, by the Habor River of Gozan, and in the towns of Media." Gozan is Tell Halaf in northeast Syria, on the Habor (Khabur) River, and Halah was near Nineveh. Chronicles uses these names for the earlier deportation of the eastern tribes (733 BC) and adds Hara, otherwise unknown; some think it comes from a form of "the mountains of Media" (hare Madai, the reading of some Greek manuscripts of Kings). "To this day" means they had not come back by the Chronicler's time, the beginning of the question of the lost tribes.

a: The sons of Levi: Gershon, Kohath and Merari.
p: Levi gets the longest list after Judah, placed in the middle of the twelve tribes. Worship is the heart of Israel.
b: Chronicles arranges the tribes with Judah first (2:3–4:23), Benjamin last (8:1–40) and Levi in the middle (6:1–81), each with the most space. These three, the tribes of the kingdom of Judah and its temple, frame all the rest. Many scholars read the arrangement as a map of the Chronicler's beliefs: David's line, the temple's servants and the people around them. Levi's list is also the most carefully organized, moving from high priests to clans, singers, the priests' duties and finally their towns. Other readers think the order simply follows the sources the writer had.

a: Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar and Ithamar
p: Nadab and Abihu are listed, though they died for offering "unauthorized fire" (Leviticus 10:1–2). The line runs through Eleazar.
b: Aaron's four sons appear as in Exodus 6:23. Nadab and Abihu died without children (Numbers 3:4), so the priesthood passed to Eleazar and Ithamar. The high-priestly line that follows runs from Eleazar; Ithamar's descendants include Eli's house, which the list skips entirely (see 24:3, where Ahimelech of Ithamar's line serves with Zadok). Miriam is named among Amram's children, one of the few women in Levi's list.

a: Eleazar fathered Phinehas
t: A high priest list with gaps
p: From Aaron to the exile, 23 names: too few for about 900 years. The list is selective, and leaves out Eli and Jehoiada.
