b: Read straight, the list gives one high priest per generation from Aaron to Jehozadak. But the Bible names high priests not in it: Eli (1 Samuel 1:9), Ahimelech and Abiathar (1 Samuel 22:20), Jehoiada (2 Kings 11:9), Uriah (2 Kings 16:10) and Azariah under Hezekiah (2 Chronicles 31:10). Some, like Eli and Abiathar, were of Ithamar's line, which the list ignores. Others may have dropped out, or the list may give a family tree, not a record of who held office. Ezra's genealogy (Ezra 7:1–5) gives a shorter form of the same line. The point is Zadok's family descending from Aaron.
r: Ezra 7:1–5; 1 Samuel 1:9; 1 Samuel 22:20; 2 Kings 11:9; 2 Kings 16:10; 2 Chronicles 31:10

a: Ahitub fathered Zadok
p: Chronicles makes Zadok a descendant of Aaron through Eleazar. Some scholars think he came from outside.
b: Zadok appears suddenly in 2 Samuel 8:17 as priest beside Abiathar, called "son of Ahitub." When Solomon banished Abiathar, Zadok's family became the only high priests in Jerusalem (1 Kings 2:35), fulfilling the word against Eli's house (1 Samuel 2:35). Ezekiel later allows only "the sons of Zadok" to serve at the altar (Ezekiel 44:15). Some modern scholars have suggested that Zadok was a Jebusite priest of Jerusalem, kept on by David, and that his link to Aaron was made later; others think the Bible's account is reliable. The rabbis took the genealogy at face value.

a: It was this Azariah who was priest in the house Solomon built in Jerusalem.
t: Which Azariah served in Solomon's temple?
p: The note seems out of place: Solomon's priest was Zadok's grandson Azariah (1 Kings 4:2), two names earlier.
b: 1 Kings 4:2 names "Azariah son of Zadok" (that is, grandson) as Solomon's priest, the Azariah of 6:9. So many think the note originally belonged after 6:9 and slipped down one line, onto the next Azariah. Others think it refers to an Azariah who stood up to King Uzziah when he tried to burn incense in the temple (2 Chronicles 26:17–18): "priest in the house" would then mean he defended its holiness. The commentary on Chronicles printed under Rashi's name takes this second view.
orig: הוּא אֲשֶׁר כִּהֵן בַּבַּיִת (hu asher kihen ba-bayit)

a: Shallum fathered Hilkiah
p: Hilkiah was the high priest who found the Book of the Law in the temple in Josiah's reign (2 Kings 22:8).
b: In 622 BC, during repairs to the temple, "Hilkiah the high priest" found the scroll that set off King Josiah's reform (2 Kings 22:8; 2 Chronicles 34:14). His grandson Seraiah was high priest when Jerusalem fell and was executed by the Babylonians at Riblah (2 Kings 25:18–21). Hilkiah's family name lived on: Ezra traces his line through Seraiah, Azariah and Hilkiah (Ezra 7:1).

a: Jehozadak went too
p: Jehozadak went into exile in 586 BC. His son Jeshua came back as high priest beside Zerubbabel.
b: The list stops at the exile, as David's line pauses at Jeconiah (3:17). The next step is told elsewhere: "Jeshua son of Jozadak" (a short form of the name) rebuilt the altar with Zerubbabel (Ezra 3:2), and Haggai and Zechariah address "Joshua son of Jehozadak, the high priest" (Haggai 1:1; Zechariah 6:11). Chronicles' first readers would have known that the priestly line, like the royal one, had survived. The Hebrew says the LORD drove Judah into exile "by the hand of" Nebuchadnezzar: the foreign king was God's instrument.

a: Gershom
p: Levi's first son is Gershon in 6:1 and the Torah, but Gershom from here on. Gershom is also Moses' son.
b: Hebrew Gershon (6:1; Exodus 6:16; Numbers 3:17) and Gershom (6:16–17, 20, 43, 62, 71; 15:7) are two spellings of one name, differing only in the last letter. Chronicles uses both, apparently following different sources. The Plain keeps each spelling where it stands. Moses' son is also Gershom (Exodus 2:22; 23:15–16), but that is a different person.

a: Amminadab his son, Korah his son
p: Korah's father is Izhar in Exodus 6:21 and in 6:38. Here he is Amminadab, a name not found among Kohath's sons.
b: Kohath's sons are Amram, Izhar, Hebron and Uzziel (6:18), and Korah is "son of Izhar" (Exodus 6:21; Numbers 16:1; 6:37–38). This verse has Amminadab instead. It may be another name for Izhar, or a scribal confusion with Amminadab, Aaron's father-in-law (Exodus 6:23). The Greek has Aminadab too. Amminadab also names a Levite head in 15:10–11.

a: The sons of Samuel: the firstborn, Joel, and the second, Abijah.
p: 1 Samuel 1:1 calls Samuel's father an Ephraimite. Chronicles places Samuel's family among the Levites.
b: Samuel's father Elkanah is "an Ephrathite" (an Ephraimite) from the hill country of Ephraim (1 Samuel 1:1), and his line there (Jeroham, Elihu, Tohu, Zuph) matches the Levite list here and in 6:33–35. Chronicles makes Samuel a Kohathite Levite, which fits his serving in the tabernacle and wearing a linen ephod (1 Samuel 2:18). Some explain "Ephraimite" as where the family lived, since Levites had towns in Ephraim (6:66–67); others think Chronicles brought the revered prophet into Levi's line. Joel and Abijah were Samuel's sons who took bribes as judges (1 Samuel 8:1–3).

a: once the ark had a place to rest
t: David the founder of temple music
p: Chronicles credits David with organizing worship in song, once the ark came to Jerusalem (15–16).
b: Samuel and Kings say little about the Levites' music; Chronicles makes it a major theme. David appoints singers when he brings the ark to Jerusalem (15:16–24; 16:4–7), organizes them into twenty-four shifts (25:1–31) and provides the instruments (23:5; 2 Chronicles 29:26). "A place to rest" echoes Psalm 132:8, "Up, LORD, to your place of rest, / you and the ark of your strength," which Solomon quotes at the temple's dedication (2 Chronicles 6:41). The ark had wandered since the wilderness; now it rested, and the Levites who had carried it could sing.

a: in front of the tabernacle, the tent of meeting
t: Song before the temple was built
p: Between David and Solomon, worship was in two places: the ark in Jerusalem, the tabernacle at Gibeon.
b: Chronicles says the old tabernacle and its altar stood at Gibeon (16:39; 21:29; 2 Chronicles 1:3), while David set the ark in a tent in Jerusalem (15:1; 16:1). The singers served "in front of the tabernacle" in the sense of the place of worship before the temple existed. Some scholars think this verse uses "tabernacle" loosely for the tent in Jerusalem. Either way, the music David began passed into Solomon's temple.

a: Heman the singer, son of Joel, son of Samuel
p: The three chief singers come from Levi's three clans. Their names stand over many psalms.
b: Heman of Kohath stood in the middle, Asaph of Gershom on the right and Ethan of Merari on the left. Twelve psalms bear Asaph's name (Psalm 50; 73–83), Psalm 88 names Heman and Psalm 89 Ethan. 1 Kings 4:31 mentions "Heman, Calcol and Darda" and "Ethan the Ezrahite" as famous wise men, sons of Mahol, perhaps the same names in a different tradition (2:6). Ethan appears to be called Jeduthun elsewhere (16:41; 25:1). Heman is Samuel's grandson: the prophet's family became a family of singers, and Chronicles calls singing prophecy (25:1).

a: son of Korah
p: Korah rebelled against Moses and died (Numbers 16), but his sons survived and became singers and gatekeepers.
b: Korah led a rebellion against Moses and Aaron and was swallowed by the earth (Numbers 16:31–33), "but the sons of Korah did not die" (Numbers 26:11). Here his descendant Heman leads the singers, and in 9:19 Korahites guard the doorway. Eleven psalms (Psalm 42; 44–49; 84–85; 87–88) carry the heading "of the sons of Korah," among them one that says, "I choose to stand at the threshold of my God's house" (Psalm 84:10), fitting for a family of gatekeepers. A rebel's line became the voice of Israel's praise.

a: Aaron and his sons, though, made the offerings go up in smoke
p: Only Aaron's descendants offered sacrifice and incense. Other Levites helped, sang and guarded.
b: Chronicles keeps the line sharp: the Levites serve "the tabernacle, the house of God" (6:48), but only Aaron's sons burn offerings, serve in the most holy place and "make atonement" (Numbers 18:1–7). When King Uzziah tried to burn incense, the priests stopped him and he was struck with skin disease (2 Chronicles 26:16–21). The Levites are not looked down on, though; Chronicles praises them, and even says they were "more upright in heart" than the priests at one point (2 Chronicles 29:34). Christian readers have often read this verse alongside Hebrews 7–10 on Christ as the one priest who makes atonement.

a: These were their places to live
p: The list of Levite towns follows Joshua 21 closely, in a different order and with some names changed.
b: Levi received no tribal land, only towns with pasture (Numbers 35:1–8; Joshua 21). Chronicles begins with Aaron's towns (Joshua 21:10–19), then gives the totals for the other clans (Joshua 21:20–40 condensed), then the towns by name. Many town names differ, mostly by spelling. Some scholars think the list reflects real towns of the kingdom era, perhaps under David or Josiah (W. F. Albright, B. Mazar); others think it is an idealized plan from the Persian period (A. G. Auld argues that Joshua 21 was based on Chronicles, not the reverse).

a: the cities of refuge, Hebron
p: The Hebrew says "the cities of refuge" though only Hebron is one. Joshua 21:13 says "the city of refuge."
b: Joshua 21:13 says they gave "Hebron, the city of refuge for killers." Chronicles has the plural, "the cities of refuge," as if all the towns that follow were cities of refuge, which they were not. It may be a simple copying change or a summary heading. The Plain keeps the plural, as in 6:67, where Shechem is the one city of refuge among several.

a: from the clan of the tribe, from half a tribe, half of Manasseh
p: Joshua 21:5 says the Kohathites got ten towns from Ephraim, Dan and half of Manasseh. Chronicles' text has lost words.
b: The Hebrew here reads awkwardly, "from the clan of the tribe, from half the tribe, half of Manasseh." Joshua has "from the clans of the tribe of Ephraim, the tribe of Dan and the half-tribe of Manasseh" (Joshua 21:5). Something has fallen out of Chronicles, probably by a scribe's eye skipping from one "tribe" to another. The Plain translates what is there, which is close to nonsense, rather than filling it in; many translations add Ephraim and Dan from Joshua. The towns from Ephraim do appear later (6:66–69), but Dan's are missing.
orig: מִמִּשְׁפַּחַת הַמַּטֶּה מִמַּחֲצִית מַטֵּה חֲצִי מְנַשֶּׁה

a: these towns that they name one by one
p: This verse summarizes Aaron's towns from Judah, Simeon and Benjamin (6:57–60), though it comes after them.
b: In Joshua 21:9 this sentence introduces the list of Aaron's towns. Chronicles opens instead with the towns (6:54–60) and puts the introduction here, after the totals. Many scholars think the writer began with Aaron's priests out of honor for them and then returned to Joshua's order; others see a later rearrangement. The Hebrew "that they call by names" means "that are listed by name."

a: Jokmeam
p: Joshua 21:22 has Kibzaim here. Jokmeam appears elsewhere as a town in the Jordan Valley.
b: The towns from Ephraim in Joshua 21:21–22 are Shechem, Gezer, Kibzaim and Beth-horon. Chronicles has Jokmeam for Kibzaim, perhaps another name for the same place, or a town of a later time. A Jokmeam is mentioned near Beth-shean in 1 Kings 4:12. Joshua 21:23–24 then lists Dan's four towns, Eltekeh, Gibbethon, Aijalon and Gath-rimmon; Chronicles puts Aijalon and Gath-rimmon here under Ephraim (6:69) and omits the other two.

a: Aner with its pastureland and Bileam
p: Joshua 21:25 has Taanach and Gath-rimmon. Bileam is probably Ibleam; Aner may be a form of Taanach.
b: Joshua 21:25 gives Manasseh's two towns as Taanach and Gath-rimmon, the second probably a copying slip from 21:24. Chronicles' Bileam matches Ibleam (Joshua 17:11; 2 Kings 9:27), a town near Taanach, and Aner may be a garbled Taanach. The Greek of Joshua has Iebatha for Gath-rimmon, which suggests the original was something like Ibleam. Chronicles may preserve the better reading.

a: Ashtaroth
p: Joshua 21:27 has Beeshterah, a contracted form of Beth-ashtaroth, "house of Ashtaroth."
b: Ashtaroth was the town of Og king of Bashan (Deuteronomy 1:4; Joshua 12:4), named for the goddess Astarte. Joshua 21:27's Be-eshterah is a short form of "Beth-ashtaroth." The towns that follow also differ from Joshua 21:28–31 in spelling: Kedesh for Kishion, Ramoth for Jarmuth, Anem for En-gannim, Mashal for Mishal, Hukok for Helkath. Most are the same towns under other spellings, though a few may be real differences.

a: Bezer in the wilderness
p: Bezer, Jahaz and other towns east of the Jordan appear on Mesha's inscription as places he took or built.
b: Mesha of Moab claims to have taken Jahaz (Hebrew here Yahtsah) and added it to his territory, and to have built Bezer "for it was in ruins" (Moabite Stone, lines 18–20, 27). Bezer was one of the six cities of refuge (Deuteronomy 4:43; Joshua 20:8). Joshua 21:36–37 has the same four Reubenite towns, which shows they belonged to Israel before Mesha's revolt in the 800s BC. By the Chronicler's time they had been Moabite for centuries, and the list is a memory.

a: Tola, Puah, Jashub and Shimron
p: Tola and Puah are also the names of a judge of Israel and his father (Judges 10:1). Jashub is Iob in Genesis 46:13.
b: "Tola son of Puah, son of Dodo, a man of Issachar" judged Israel twenty-three years (Judges 10:1–2). Using the names of the clan founders for a later hero was common. Genesis 46:13 calls the third son Iob; Numbers 26:24 and Chronicles have Jashub, which is probably the older form. The Hebrew Ketiv here spells it Jashib; the Plain follows the Qere, Jashub.

a: in David's days their number was 22,600
p: The northern tribes' lists in chapter 7 read like army rolls, giving fighting men by clan.
b: Unlike Judah's and Levi's lists, chapter 7 counts "strong warriors" and gives totals. The numbers may come from census records like David's (21:1–6; 27:23–24) or from military rolls of the northern kingdom. They are large (Issachar: 22,600 + 36,000 + 87,000), and some suggest that elef, "thousand," here means a unit (see 5:21). "In David's days" ties the record to the one time all twelve tribes were united under Judah's king.

a: Benjamin: Bela, Becher and Jediael, three.
p: Benjamin is listed here and again in chapter 8, while Zebulun and Dan get no list. Some think this was once Zebulun's.
b: Chronicles mentions Zebulun only in passing (2:1; 6:63, 77) and gives no list for Dan. Benjamin appears here and again, much more fully, in chapter 8. Several scholars have suggested that 7:6–11 was originally Zebulun's list, the name damaged in copying, since its place after Issachar matches Zebulun's usual place. Others note that the names (Bela, Becher) are Benjaminite (Genesis 46:21) and think the writer simply had two Benjamin sources. Either way, the missing tribes show the writer worked from the records he had, not a tidy plan.

a: Hushim, the sons of Aher
p: Genesis 46:23 says Dan's son was Hushim. "Aher" means "another," perhaps standing in for Dan's name.
b: Dan has no list in Chronicles, but the only son of Dan in Genesis is Hushim (Genesis 46:23; Shuham in Numbers 26:42). After this verse comes Naphtali, and Dan and Naphtali are the two sons of Bilhah, named together in 7:13. So many scholars think this half-verse is all that remains of Dan's list, and that acher, "another," either replaced Dan's name or is a damaged "Dan." Rabbinic tradition said Dan was left out because of the idol of Micah and the shrine at Dan (Judges 18). Others read Aher simply as an unknown Benjaminite.

a: Jahziel, Guni, Jezer and Shallum
p: Genesis 46:24 has Jahzeel and Shillem. Chronicles' Jahziel and Shallum are spelling variants.
b: Naphtali's four sons are the same as in Genesis 46:24 and Numbers 26:48–49, with Chronicles' spellings Jahziel (for Jahzeel) and Shallum (for Shillem). The verse ends "Bilhah's descendants," grouping Naphtali with Dan (7:12) as the sons of Rachel's servant Bilhah.

a: born to him by his Aramean concubine
p: Manasseh's son Machir is born of an Aramean woman. East of the Jordan, Israel and Aram mixed.
b: Machir was the ancestor of the Gileadites (Numbers 26:29), and his clans lived east of the Jordan, next to Aram. Naming his mother an Aramean reflects that border world. The verse is hard: in Numbers 26:31, Asriel is Gilead's son, not Manasseh's, and the sentence seems to have lost a word or two. 2:21–23 also tells how Hezron of Judah married a daughter of Machir.

a: The second one's name was Zelophehad, and Zelophehad had daughters.
p: Zelophehad had only daughters. Their case set the law that daughters can inherit (Numbers 27:1–11).
b: Mahlah, Noa, Hoglah, Milcah and Tirzah went to Moses and asked for their father's land, and God answered, "Zelophehad's daughters have spoken rightly" (Numbers 27:7). The law that followed let daughters inherit when there was no son. Chronicles simply notes the daughters, assuming the reader knew the story. Verse 15 is badly damaged: "his sister was named Maacah" clashes with 7:16, where Maacah is Machir's wife, and "the second" has no first. One of the daughters, Mahlah, may be the Mahlah of 7:18.

a: Bedan
p: Bedan is also the name of a deliverer in the Hebrew of 1 Samuel 12:11, where the Greek reads Barak.
b: In Samuel's farewell speech the Hebrew lists the LORD's deliverers as "Jerubbaal, Bedan, Jephthah and Samuel" (1 Samuel 12:11, Hebrew). No judge called Bedan is known, and the Greek and Syriac read Barak there; the site's Plain of 1 Samuel follows Barak. The rabbis identified Bedan with Samson ("son of Dan," ben Dan). This Bedan, a grandson of Gilead, shows the name was real in Manasseh. It may be that 1 Samuel's Bedan was a Gileadite hero whose story is lost.

a: Hammolecheth bore Ishhod, Abiezer and Mahlah
p: Abiezer was Gideon's clan (Judges 6:11). The family list names its ancestress, Hammolecheth, "the queen."
b: Gideon was an Abiezrite (Judges 6:11), and he protested, "my clan is the poorest in Manasseh, and in my father's house I count for least" (Judges 6:15). Joshua 17:2 lists Abiezer as a clan of Manasseh, as here. Hammolekhet means "the one who reigns" or "the queen"; the Targum made her a woman who ruled part of Gilead. Mahlah is also the name of one of Zelophehad's daughters (Numbers 26:33), perhaps the same clan.

a: The men of Gath, who were born in the land, killed them, because they went down to take their herds.
p: Ephraim's sons died raiding the cattle of Gath. When did this happen, if Ephraim lived in Egypt?
b: Genesis has Ephraim born and dying in Egypt (Genesis 41:52; 50:22–23), yet here he mourns sons killed in a raid on Gath in Canaan. (1) Jewish tradition told of Ephraimites who left Egypt thirty years before the exodus and were slaughtered by Philistines; their bones lay in the road, and God led Israel the long way so they would not see them and lose heart (Bavli Sanhedrin 92b; Targum Pseudo-Jonathan on Exodus 13:17). (2) Many modern scholars think this preserves a clan tradition of Ephraimites who never went to Egypt, or that "Ephraim" is the tribe, mourning later losses. (3) Some take "Ephraim" as a later descendant who bore the ancestor's name. Gath here is probably Gittaim near Ephraim's border, not the Philistine city.

a: his brothers came to comfort him
p: The scene echoes Jacob mourning Joseph: his children came to comfort him, but he refused (Genesis 37:35).
b: When Jacob thought Joseph was dead, "he mourned for his son for many days" and "All his sons and all his daughters came to comfort him" (Genesis 37:34–35). Ephraim, Joseph's son, now mourns his own sons in almost the same words. The genealogy pauses to show a family's grief, a rare human moment in these lists.

a: He named him Beriah, because trouble had come on his house.
p: The name Beriah is explained as be-ra'ah, "in trouble." A child born after tragedy carries its memory.
b: The father explains the name as be-ra'ah, "in evil, in disaster," a wordplay on Beri'ah. Like Jabez (4:9) and Rachel's son Ben-oni, "son of my sorrow" (Genesis 35:18), the child's name remembers pain. Beriah is also the name of a son of Asher (7:30) and a Benjaminite (8:13), where the sound-play does not apply. From this son of grief came Joshua (7:27).

a: She built Beth-horon, Lower and Upper
p: Sheerah is the only woman in the Bible said to have built a town. Three places are credited to her.
b: Building towns is usually the work of kings (2 Chronicles 8:5, where Solomon builds the same Beth-horons) or clan founders (8:12). Sheerah, Ephraim's daughter or granddaughter, built three: Lower and Upper Beth-horon, which guarded the main road up from the coast to Jerusalem, and Uzzen-sheerah, "Sheerah's ear" (or "corner"), named for her. "Built" may mean founded or fortified. Her name stands out in a list that otherwise names men.

a: Non his son, Joshua his son.
p: Joshua son of Nun appears with his whole ancestry, ten generations from Ephraim. The Hebrew spells Nun as Non.
b: Elsewhere Joshua is only "son of Nun" (Exodus 33:11; Numbers 13:8). Here the genealogy gives his ancestors, including "Elishama son of Ammihud," Ephraim's leader at the first census (Numbers 1:10; 7:48). The Hebrew spells Nun as Non in this verse only, and the Plain keeps the spelling. Joshua was Moses' assistant and successor, who led Israel into the land. His place at the end of Ephraim's line, like David's at the end of Judah's, gives the list its point.

a: Beth-shean and its villages, Taanach and its villages, Megiddo and its villages, and Dor
p: These four towns were Manasseh's on paper, but Judges 1:27 says Manasseh did not drive out their people.
b: Joshua 17:11–12 and Judges 1:27 list Beth-shean, Taanach, Dor and Megiddo (with Ibleam) as towns Manasseh received but could not conquer, "The Canaanites were set on living in that land" (Judges 1:27). Chronicles gives them as the sons of Joseph's home without comment. By Solomon's time these were Israelite towns (1 Kings 4:12), and archaeology shows Megiddo and Taanach as major cities of the northern kingdom.

a: and their sister Serah
p: Serah appears in every list of Asher's family. Jewish legend made her live for centuries, from Joseph to David.
b: Serah is named in Genesis 46:17 and Numbers 26:46, one of very few granddaughters of Jacob mentioned. Because she appears in both the going down to Egypt and the census at the end of the wilderness, the rabbis gave her a long life. She was said to have gently told Jacob that Joseph was alive by singing to him, and was blessed with long life; she showed Moses where Joseph's bones were buried; and some identified her with the "wise woman" of Abel who saved her city in David's day (2 Samuel 20:16–22; Genesis Rabbah 94:9). Some legends say she entered paradise alive.

a: picked men, strong warriors, chiefs among the leaders
t: The language of a muster roll
p: Barur, "picked," and the count "for service in war" sound like an army register.
b: Berurim, "picked, chosen," is used of the gatekeepers in 9:22 and of David's singers in 16:41. Combined with "strong warriors" and the count "for the army, for war," the verse reads like the heading of a military roll. Asher's 26,000 is far below its numbers in Numbers (41,500 and 53,400), which may show the list is from a different period, when the tribe was smaller.

a: Benjamin fathered Bela his firstborn, Ashbel the second, Aharah the third,
p: Genesis 46:21 lists ten sons; Numbers 26:38–39 five; Chronicles three in 7:6 and five here. Names differ in every list.
b: Genesis 46:21: Bela, Becher, Ashbel, Gera, Naaman, Ehi, Rosh, Muppim, Huppim, Ard. Numbers 26:38–40: Bela, Ashbel, Ahiram, Shephupham, Hupham, with Ard and Naaman as Bela's sons. Chronicles 8:1–2: Bela, Ashbel, Aharah, Nohah, Rapha. Aharah may be Ahiram; others are hard to match. The lists likely reflect clans that rose and fell over centuries, with grandsons counted as sons. They are not contradictions so much as snapshots.

a: These were the sons of Ehud.
p: Ehud son of Gera, the left-handed judge (Judges 3:15), belonged to Benjamin. These clans lived in Geba.
b: Judges 3:15 calls the deliverer Ehud "son of Gera, a Benjaminite, a left-handed man." Gera appears twice in this list (8:3, 5), which fits. Whether this Ehud is the judge is uncertain; the text does not say how Ehud connects to Bela's sons. Geba was a Levite town in Benjamin (6:60). The exile to Manahath is unknown; it may be a clan conflict or a move to a place near Jerusalem (2:52, 54).

a: In the fields of Moab, after he had sent off his wives Hushim and Baara
p: Shaharaim lived in Moab and divorced two wives. Some of his sons have Moabite names, such as Mesha.
b: Benjaminites and Moabites shared a border along the Jordan, and families crossed it. David's great-grandmother Ruth was a Moabite, and David took his parents to Moab for safety (1 Samuel 22:3–4). One of Shaharaim's sons is named Mesha, like the Moabite king of the Moabite Stone (2 Kings 3:4), and Malcam recalls Milcom, the god of Ammon. "Sent off" is the verb used for divorce (Deuteronomy 24:1). Hushim, though sent away, is named as mother of two sons in 8:11.

a: Shemed built Ono and Lod with its villages.
p: Lod is the Lydda of Acts, where Peter healed Aeneas. Ono and Lod were resettled after the exile.
b: The returning exiles included "the people of Lod, Hadid and Ono" (Ezra 2:33; Nehemiah 7:37), and Nehemiah's enemies tried to lure him to "the plain of Ono" (Nehemiah 6:2). Lod became Lydda, where Peter healed the paralyzed Aeneas (Acts 9:32–35), and is today's Lod near Tel Aviv's airport. Egyptian lists of the 1400s BC already mention Lod and Ono, so they were old towns that a clan of Benjamin refounded.

a: They drove out the people living in Gath.
p: Benjaminites of Aijalon drove out the people of Gath, perhaps avenging Ephraim's sons (7:21).
b: Aijalon guarded the valley where Joshua made the sun stand still (Joshua 10:12). Benjaminites living there drove out the people of Gath, probably Gittaim, a town near Benjamin's western border (2 Samuel 4:3; Nehemiah 11:33), rather than Philistine Gath. Some connect this with the story in 7:21: since Ephraim named a son Beriah after that disaster, and these leaders include a Beriah, the two notes may preserve one clan tradition of conflict with Gath.

a: They lived in Jerusalem.
p: Jerusalem lay on the border of Judah and Benjamin, and Benjamin shared the city.
b: Joshua 18:28 lists Jebus, "which is Jerusalem," among Benjamin's towns, and Joshua 15:8 places the border of Judah just south of it. As for the Jebusites living there, "the Benjaminites did not drive them out" (Judges 1:21). After the exile, Benjaminites again lived in Jerusalem (9:3–9; Nehemiah 11:7–9). The note bridges to Saul's family, which also had a branch in Jerusalem (8:32).

a: In Gibeon lived the father of Gibeon
p: Saul's ancestors are traced to Gibeon, the city of the Gibeonites Saul tried to wipe out (2 Samuel 21:1–2).
b: Saul came from Gibeah, a few miles from Gibeon (1 Samuel 10:26), and Gibeon was a city of non-Israelite Hivites who tricked Joshua into a treaty (Joshua 9). That Saul's family should be rooted in Gibeon is striking, given that Saul, "burning with zeal for Israel and Judah, had tried to strike them down" (2 Samuel 21:2). Some think a Benjaminite clan settled in Gibeon and took the name "father of Gibeon" as its founder. In 9:35 the father is named Jeiel; this verse lacks the name (see the variant).

a: Ner fathered Kish, and Kish fathered Saul.
t: Kish, son of Ner or of Abiel?
p: 1 Samuel 9:1 calls Kish the son of Abiel, and 14:51 makes Ner Kish's brother. Chronicles makes Ner Kish's father.
b: 1 Samuel 9:1 gives "Kish son of Abiel," and 1 Samuel 14:50–51 says Saul's army commander was "Abner son of Ner, Saul's uncle," and "Kish was the father of Saul. Ner, the father of Abner, was a son of Abiel" (1 Samuel 14:50–51). That makes Ner Saul's uncle. Chronicles here and in 9:39 says Ner was Saul's grandfather. (1) "Saul's uncle" in 1 Samuel 14:50 may describe Abner, not Ner; then Ner is Kish's father, as here, and "son of Abiel" means a more distant descendant. (2) Some think there were two men named Ner or Kish (8:30; 9:36). (3) Others accept that the traditions differ. Abiel and Jeiel (9:35) may be the same man.

a: Esh-baal
p: 2 Samuel calls Saul's son Ish-bosheth, "man of shame." Chronicles keeps his real name, Esh-baal.
b: Esh-ba'al means "man of the Lord" or "the Lord exists," using ba'al, "lord, master," which could be a title of the LORD in early Israel. Later scribes, uneasy with the word after it became the name of the Canaanite god Baal, replaced it with bosheth, "shame": Ish-bosheth (2 Samuel 2:8). Chronicles kept the older forms, here and for Merib-baal (8:34). See the note on 2 Samuel 2:8. 1 Samuel 14:49 lists Saul's sons as Jonathan, Ishvi and Malchishua; Ishvi may be another name for Esh-baal.

a: Jonathan's son was Merib-baal
p: Merib-baal is Mephibosheth, Jonathan's lame son whom David took in. His line went on for generations.
b: 2 Samuel calls him Mephibosheth (2 Samuel 4:4; 2 Samuel 9:6), another case of baal replaced by bosheth. David "kept loyal love" with Jonathan by giving him a place at his table (2 Samuel 9:1–13), and he "had a little son called Mica" (2 Samuel 9:12). Chronicles shows that Micah's line continued for about ten more generations, down to Ulam's grandsons (8:40). Saul's house lost the throne but not its place in Israel. The spelling Meri-baal in 9:40 may mean "the Lord is my advocate."

a: strong warriors who bent the bow
p: Benjamin was famous for skilled fighters: left-handed slingers, archers, and men who shot with either hand.
b: Judges 20:16 tells of 700 left-handed Benjaminites who "could hit a single hair with a slingstone, never missing" (Judges 20:16), and the Benjaminites who joined David at Ziklag could sling stones and shoot arrows with either hand (12:2). Saul and Jonathan were archers (2 Samuel 1:22). Saul's family ends as it began, with fighting men, and the line runs on to the 150 descendants of Ulam, perhaps into the Chronicler's own time.

a: All Israel, then, was enrolled in family registers
p: The genealogies end by naming their goal: all Israel enrolled, an exile caused by unfaithfulness, and a return.
b: The verse sums up chapters 1–8 and introduces the returned community. Why the long lists? (1) Identity: after the exile, Israel needed to know who belonged, especially priests and Levites (Ezra 2:59–63). (2) Unity: all twelve tribes are included, though only Judah, Benjamin and Levi returned in numbers; the Chronicler hopes for all Israel. (3) Continuity: the same families run from Adam to the return, so the returned community is the true Israel. (4) Theology: David's line and Levi's service are at the center. Marshall Johnson and Robert Wilson showed that ancient genealogies served such purposes more than preserving history for its own sake.

a: the Book of the Kings of Israel. And Judah
t: Israel's book, or the Kings of Israel and Judah?
p: The Masoretic accents end the sentence at "Israel"; many versions read "the Book of the Kings of Israel and Judah."
b: Elsewhere Chronicles cites "the Book of the Kings of Judah and Israel" or "of Israel and Judah" (2 Chronicles 16:11; 27:7). So many read here "the book of the kings of Israel and Judah. They were carried off..." (so KJV, BSB). The Masoretic accents divide the verse after "Israel," making Judah the subject of the next sentence: "And Judah was carried off." The Plain follows the accents. Either way, the book named was a source the writer used.
orig: סֵפֶר מַלְכֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל וִיהוּדָה (sefer malkhe Yisra'el vi-Yhudah)

a: because of their unfaithfulness
p: Ma'al, "unfaithfulness," is Chronicles' word for the sin that led to exile, from Achar (2:7) to the last king.
b: The noun and verb ma'al mean breaking faith with God, often in holy matters. Chronicles uses it at key points: Achar (2:7), the eastern tribes (5:25), Saul (10:13), Uzziah (2 Chronicles 26:16), Ahaz (2 Chronicles 28:19) and the leaders at the end (2 Chronicles 36:14). Leviticus 26:40 promises that if Israel confesses its ma'al, God will remember his covenant. The genealogies thus begin the story of return by naming the cause of exile.

a: the servants given to the temple
p: The Nethinim, "those given," were temple servants. The rabbis linked them with the Gibeonites Joshua made woodcutters.
b: Netinim appears only here and in Ezra–Nehemiah, where 392 of them return with their "sons of Solomon's servants" (Ezra 2:43–58). Ezra 8:20 says David "gave" them to serve the Levites. The rabbis identified them with the Gibeonites, whom Joshua "made" woodcutters and water-carriers for the altar (Joshua 9:27), and held that their status passed to their children (Bavli Yevamot 78b–79a). Many of their names in Ezra are foreign, which suggests captives or foreigners attached to the temple. This translation calls them "the servants given to the temple."

a: The first inhabitants
t: First to return, or former inhabitants?
p: Ha-rishonim can mean "the first" to settle after the exile or "the former" inhabitants, before it.
b: The Hebrew ha-yoshevim ha-rishonim is literally "the first inhabitants." Most readers take it as the first to settle in Jerusalem and the towns after the return, which fits Nehemiah 11:3 and the list that follows. A minority read "the former inhabitants," the people who lived there before the exile, so that the list would describe the old order the returned community restored. The Plain keeps "first" and leaves the question open.

a: and some from Ephraim and Manasseh
p: Nehemiah 11 lists only Judah and Benjamin. Chronicles adds Ephraim and Manasseh: the north, too, came back.
b: The list of 9:2–17 is closely related to Nehemiah 11:3–19, but the two differ in many names and numbers. Chronicles' mention of Ephraim and Manasseh, with no names given for them, is not in Nehemiah. It fits the Chronicler's hope that "all Israel" belongs to Jerusalem: in his story, northerners keep coming south to worship (2 Chronicles 11:16; 15:9; 30:11, 18). Some scholars think 9:2–34 is the Chronicler's own reworking of Nehemiah 11; others think both drew on a common list.

a: son of Bani, of the sons of Perez
p: The written Hebrew (Ketiv) reads Benjamin here; the reading tradition (Qere) divides it as "Bani, of."
b: The consonants bnymn spell "Benjamin," which would make Uthai's ancestor a Benjamin among the sons of Perez of Judah. The Masoretes' Qere divides the letters as Bani min, "Bani, of (the sons of Perez)," which fits the line and Judah's place in the verse. The Plain follows the Qere, as it does throughout (see the note on 1:46).
orig: Ketiv בִּנְיָמִן (Binyamin); Qere בָּנִי מִן (Bani min)

a: Of the Shilonites
p: The Hebrew says Shilonites, people from Shiloh, but Judah's clans are Perez, Zerah and Shelah. Shelanites is likely meant.
b: Judah had three sons who had children: Perez (9:4), Zerah (9:6) and Shelah (2:3; 4:21). The Shelanites are Shelah's clan (Numbers 26:20). The Masoretic vowels read ha-Shiloni, "the Shilonite," as if from Shiloh, but the consonants allow ha-Shelani. Most scholars think the Shelanites are meant; Nehemiah 11:5 has "son of the Shilonite" too. The Plain follows the Masoretic vowels.

a: Jedaiah, Jehoiarib, Jachin
p: Jedaiah and Jehoiarib head two of the twenty-four priestly shifts (24:7). The Maccabees came from Jehoiarib.
b: In David's arrangement of the priests, the first lot fell to Jehoiarib and the second to Jedaiah (24:7). Mattathias, father of Judas Maccabeus, was "a priest of the line of Joarib" (1 Maccabees 2:1), the first of the twenty-four, so the Hasmonean rulers traced their family to this list. Jachin was the twenty-first course (24:17).

a: the officer in charge of the house of God
p: The word nagid, used for David as God's "ruler," here means the chief officer of the temple.
b: Nagid means a leader appointed from above. It is David's title as God's chosen ruler (5:2; 11:2), but it also names officials: "the officer in charge of the house of God" (here; 2 Chronicles 31:13; Jeremiah 20:1, where Pashhur held the post). Phinehas was nagid over the gatekeepers (9:20). This translation says "ruler" for the king and "officer in charge" for others. Azariah here is the same man as Seraiah in Nehemiah 11:11, probably by a name change in one of the lists.

p: Nehemiah counts 1,192 priests in three groups; Chronicles 1,760. Lists from different times, or copying changes.
b: Nehemiah 11:12–14 gives 822 + 242 + 128 = 1,192 priests. Chronicles has 1,760. Judah's 690 (9:6) compares with Nehemiah's 468 Perezites (11:6), and Benjamin's 956 (9:9) with 928 (11:8). The names also differ. The two lists may describe the community at different times, or the Chronicler may have updated an older list. They show the same thing: a small community, with a large share of priests.

a: The gatekeepers were Shallum, Akkub, Talmon and Ahiman
p: Ezra 2:42 lists gatekeepers apart from Levites. Chronicles counts them as Levites with an ancient role.
b: Ezra 2:40–42 and Nehemiah 7:43–45 list Levites, then singers, then gatekeepers as separate groups. Nehemiah 11:19 names Akkub and Talmon as gatekeepers. Chronicles insists the gatekeepers are Levites (9:26), going back to the wilderness, when Levites guarded the tent (9:19; Numbers 3:32). Many scholars see a development: singers and gatekeepers were gradually counted among the Levites in the Persian period, and the Chronicler supports their place. Others think Chronicles preserves an old reality that Ezra's list simply separates for counting.

a: the King's Gate, facing east
p: The King's Gate on the east was the king's entrance to the temple. Ezekiel 46 gives the prince an eastern gate.
b: In the time of the kings, the king had his own entrance to the temple (2 Kings 16:18), and in Ezekiel's vision the east gate was kept shut, opened only for the prince (Ezekiel 44:1–3; 46:1–2). After the exile there was no king, but the gate kept its name, and the chief gatekeeper's family guarded it "to this day." East was the direction the temple faced, so this was the main entrance.

a: The LORD was with him.
p: "The LORD was with him" can also be read as a prayer: "May the LORD be with him."
b: Phinehas, Aaron's grandson, was promised "a covenant of lasting priesthood" for his zeal at Baal-peor (Numbers 25:11–13). Here he is remembered as nagid over the Levite guards. The Hebrew phrase has no verb, so it can be read as a statement or a blessing: "May the LORD be with him." In later Jewish usage the formula became a way of honoring a revered figure. Phinehas guarded the holy place in the wilderness (Numbers 25:7–8), which fits his place as head of the gatekeepers.

a: David and Samuel the seer had put them in their posts
p: Samuel died before David became king. Here they set up the gatekeepers together.
b: Samuel died while David was still on the run from Saul (1 Samuel 25:1), so the two never ran the sanctuary together. (1) Some read this as a pious memory, placing the founding of the gatekeepers' order under Israel's two great founders. (2) Others note that Samuel served at Shiloh's sanctuary with its doorkeepers (1 Samuel 3:15) and might have begun an arrangement David finished. (3) Rabbinic sources had Samuel and David plan the temple together at Ramah (1 Samuel 19:18; Bavli Zevachim 54b). "Seer" (ro'eh) is an old word for prophet (1 Samuel 9:9).

a: for seven days at a time
p: Levites from the villages came to serve one week at a time. Zechariah, John the Baptist's father, served this way.
b: The rota of a week at a time (2 Kings 11:5–9; 2 Chronicles 23:8) let families who lived in villages around Jerusalem share the work. In the first century, priests still served by divisions: when Zechariah "was doing his work as a priest before God, when his division's turn came round" (Luke 1:8), he was chosen by lot to burn incense, and then went home (Luke 1:23).

a: they were in charge of the key, morning after morning
p: The gatekeepers spent the night at the temple and opened it each morning. The key became a picture of authority.
b: Isaiah 22:22 says God would give Eliakim "the key of the house of David": what he opened, no one would shut. Revelation 3:7 applies the image to Christ, "who holds the key of David" (Revelation 3:7), and Jesus gives Peter "the keys of the kingdom" (Matthew 16:19). In the Mishnah, the priests' elders slept in a chamber near the temple's gates and kept its keys, opening them each dawn (Mishnah Tamid 1:1). Opening the gates was the start of each day's worship.

a: Some of the sons of the priests mixed the blend of spices.
p: Levites kept the spices, but only priests could mix the holy blend (Exodus 30:34–38).
b: Exodus 30:22–38 gives the recipes for the anointing oil and the incense and forbids anyone to make them for private use. Chronicles is careful: Levites have charge of supplies (9:29), but mixing the blend is a priestly task. In the Second Temple period the family of Avtinas held the secret of the incense (Mishnah Yoma 3:11).

a: the bread that is set out in rows
p: Twelve loaves were set out on the gold table every Sabbath (Leviticus 24:5–9). Jesus mentions David eating them.
b: The Hebrew is lechem ha-ma'arakhet, "bread of the row," a later name for what Exodus calls the Presence Bread (Exodus 25:30). Twelve loaves, one for each tribe, were set in two rows on the table and replaced every Sabbath; the old loaves were eaten by priests (Leviticus 24:5–9). David once ate them when fleeing Saul (1 Samuel 21:6), and Jesus cited that story about the Sabbath (Mark 2:25–26). Kohathites had carried the table in the wilderness (Numbers 4:7).

a: because they were at their work day and night
p: The singers were on duty day and night. Psalm 134 calls on those who "stand in the LORD's house by night."
b: Psalm 134:1 blesses the servants of the LORD "who stand in the LORD's house at night." Chronicles imagines praise that never stops, and the singers are freed from other work for it. Revelation pictures the same around God's throne: "day and night they never stop saying, 'Holy, holy, holy'" (Revelation 4:8). Christian monastic orders later took up the idea in the cycle of prayer through the day and night.

a: In Gibeon lived the father of Gibeon, Jeiel
p: 9:35–44 repeats 8:29–38, to lead into Saul's death in chapter 10. The two copies differ in small ways.
b: The repetition makes a bridge: the genealogies end, and the story begins with Saul's last battle (10:1). Comparing the two copies shows how names were copied: 9:35 has Jeiel, which 8:29 lacks; 9:36–37 add Ner and Mikloth; 8:32 has Shimeah, 9:38 Shimeam; 9:40 has Meri-baal for Merib-baal; 8:36 Jehoaddah, 9:42 Jarah; 8:37 Raphah, 9:43 Rephaiah. Each copy helps restore the other. Saul's line is given in full just before Chronicles reports that God turned the kingdom over to David (10:14).

a: Ahaz fathered Jarah
p: 8:36 has Jehoaddah; 9:42 has Jarah. The Hebrew letters of the two names are easily confused.
b: Yeho'addah (8:36) and Ya'rah (9:42) look different in English, but in Hebrew script the d and r look nearly alike, and the forms differ by only a few letters. The Greek of both places reads something like Iada, and many scholars think the original was Jehoaddah or Jaddah. The Plain gives each verse as it stands.
